title: Preconception Health Checklist: Essential Steps Before Getting Pregnant
excerpt: Planning for a baby starts well before conception. Here is an essential medical checklist covering folic acid, blood tests, dental care, and lifestyle changes for Indian couples.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Planning for Pregnancy: Where to Begin

The journey to parenthood begins long before you see two pink lines on a home test kit. Optimizing your maternal health before conception significantly reduces risks of complications such as neural tube defects, gestational hypertension, and maternal anaemia.

1. Start Folic Acid Supplementation

Gynecologists strongly recommend taking 400 to 500 mcg of folic acid daily starting at least 1 to 3 months before attempting conception. Folic acid plays an indispensable role in neural tube development during the very first 28 days of gestation—often before a woman even realizes she is pregnant.

2. Schedule a Pre-Pregnancy Health Checkup

Consult with your OBGYN for pre-pregnancy blood screenings:

  • Complete Blood Count (CBC) & Haemoglobin: Anemia is remarkably common among Indian women and should be corrected early.
  • Rubella & Hepatitis B Immunity: Testing antibodies ensures protection against infections that can adversely impact fetal organ development.
  • Blood Sugar (HbA1c / Fasting Glucose): Early detection of prediabetes or insulin resistance allows for dietary calibration prior to pregnancy.
  • Thyroid Profile (TSH): Maternal thyroid health is crucial for early embryonic neurodevelopment.

3. Review Current Medications

Certain routine medications for acne, blood pressure, or migraines are contraindicated during pregnancy. Never stop prescribed therapies abruptly; instead, discuss pregnancy-safe alternatives with your doctor.

4. Dental Evaluation

Hormonal surges in pregnancy exacerbate gum inflammation and gingivitis. Periodontal infection has been clinically linked with preterm labour. Undergoing a thorough dental cleaning and addressing cavities beforehand ensures safety.

5. Healthy Weight & Diet Adjustments

Achieving a balanced body mass index (BMI) promotes regular ovulation. Emphasize home-cooked Indian meals rich in lentils, seasonal green vegetables, paneer, eggs, seeds, and nuts while limiting excess refined sugar and trans-fats.

content:
Those two weeks after ovulation can feel like the longest wait ever! You may find yourself checking your body for every little sign, wondering if that mild cramp means something, or feeling tempted to take a pregnancy test even before your period is due.

And when the result is negative, you may wonder if you tested too early.

If this sounds familiar, you're not alone. The wait can be exciting, confusing and sometimes stressful. But knowing when to test, what the result means and when to test again can make things a little easier.

Let's understand it step by step.

Why do I keep testing even though I know it's too early?

When you're hoping for a positive result, waiting can be really difficult. Taking a pregnancy test gives you a feeling that you're doing something, even when you know it may be too early.

But remember, testing again and again won't make the pregnancy hormone (hCG) appear any faster. It may only leave you dealing with repeated negative results and unnecessary stress.

Try choosing a date to test—ideally the first day your period is due or after it is missed. Until then, give yourself a little break from testing. You deserve to enjoy these days too.

Am I imagining pregnancy symptoms, or are they real this early?

Tender breasts, bloating, tiredness, mild cramps and mood changes can make you wonder if you're pregnant.

But here's the tricky part: these symptoms can happen before your period too!

After ovulation, your body produces progesterone whether you're pregnant or not. This hormone can cause many symptoms that feel just like early pregnancy signs.

So don't worry if you're noticing symptoms, or if you're not feeling anything at all. Neither can reliably tell you whether you're pregnant. A pregnancy test taken at the right time is a much better way to find out.

How does a pregnancy test actually detect pregnancy?

A pregnancy test looks for a hormone called hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) in your urine.

Your body starts producing this hormone after the fertilised egg attaches to the lining of your uterus. In the beginning, the levels are very low, but they rise as early pregnancy progresses.

A home pregnancy test detects hCG once it reaches a certain level in your urine. If you test too early, there may simply not be enough hormone for the test to pick up.

That's why a negative result in the early days doesn't always mean you're not pregnant.

Can you take a pregnancy test before a missed period?

Yes! Some pregnancy tests are sensitive enough to detect pregnancy a few days before your expected period.

But there's a catch: if you test too early, you may get a negative result even if you're pregnant.

This happens because your hCG levels may not have risen enough yet.

If you can wait, it's better to test from the first day of your missed period. You'll have a much better chance of getting a reliable result.

What does a faint line actually mean?

You've taken the test, and there's a second line—but it's so light that you're not sure whether it's positive!

Don't panic. A faint coloured line that appears within the time mentioned in the test instructions usually means a positive result. It may simply be that your hCG levels are still low because it's very early in pregnancy.

A faint line does not automatically mean something is wrong.

If you're unsure, repeat the test after 48 hours or speak to your doctor. Remember to follow the instructions of your particular test kit.

Positive line or evaporation line—how do you tell the difference?

This is one of the most confusing parts of home pregnancy testing.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

  • A positive line: A coloured second line (even if faint) appears within the reading time mentioned in the instructions.
  • An evaporation line: A faint, often colourless or grey mark may appear after the test has dried, outside the recommended reading time.

The most important thing is to read your test within the time mentioned on the packet. Don't go back and check the same strip an hour later, as the result may no longer be reliable.

If you're still confused, use a fresh test or consult your doctor.

What happens if you test too early?

The most common problem is a false negative.

This means your test says you're not pregnant, even though you may actually be pregnant. It usually happens because your hCG levels are still too low to be detected.

So, if you test early and get a negative result, don't lose hope just yet.

Wait a few days and test again, especially if your period hasn't arrived.

What is the best day to actually take a pregnancy test?

For most women, the best time to take a home pregnancy test is from the first day of a missed period.

For a more reliable result:

  • Use your first-morning urine, especially if you're testing early.
  • Check that your test kit hasn't expired.
  • Follow the instructions carefully.
  • Read the result only within the recommended time.

You don't necessarily need morning urine once your period is overdue, but it can help when hCG levels are still low.

Does an irregular cycle make it harder to know when to test?

Absolutely! If your periods are irregular, it can be difficult to know whether your period is actually late or simply delayed.

You may have ovulated later than usual, which also means pregnancy hormone levels may take longer to become detectable.

If you don't know when your next period is due, a useful rule is to take a pregnancy test at least 21 days after unprotected sex.

If you're tracking ovulation, that information can also help you decide when to test.

Why does everyone suddenly want to know if you have good news?

If you're trying to conceive, you probably know how this goes!

A family member asks, "Any good news?" Someone at work wants to know if you're pregnant yet. And sometimes, even before you have an answer yourself, everyone seems to be waiting for one.

Remember, you don't have to share anything until you're ready.

You can simply say, "We'll let you know when there's something to share."

Your pregnancy journey is personal. Give yourself the time and space you need.

Negative test, but still no period—what should you do?

A negative pregnancy test with no period can be confusing. But there can be several reasons for this:

  • You may have tested too early.
  • You may have ovulated later than expected.
  • Stress, illness, travel or hormonal changes may have delayed your period.

If your test is negative but your period still hasn't arrived, wait 2–3 days and repeat the test.

If the second test is also negative and your period hasn't come, consult your gynaecologist. Your doctor may recommend a blood hCG test or further evaluation depending on your situation.

When should you stop testing and call your doctor?

If you've taken repeated home tests and still don't have a clear answer, there's no need to keep buying test kits and worrying.

Speak to your gynaecologist. A blood hCG test can help clarify whether you're pregnant, and your doctor can guide you on what to do next.

If you have severe abdominal pain, particularly on one side, heavy bleeding, dizziness or fainting, seek urgent medical attention—even if your home pregnancy test is negative.

A little reminder before you go: The two-week wait can feel long, but you don't have to spend every day looking for signs. Give your body time, test at the right moment and be kind to yourself. Whatever the result, take the next step with the right guidance and support.

Your journey, your pace. We're with you.

content:
Seeing blood or spotting after finding out you're pregnant can be scary. You may immediately wonder if something is wrong with your baby. But take a breath. Light spotting can happen in early pregnancy, and many women who experience it go on to have healthy pregnancies.

However, spotting should never be ignored. Sometimes it can be an early sign of a problem that needs medical attention. The important thing is to know what could be causing it, which symptoms to watch for and when to contact your doctor.

Let's understand it without unnecessary panic.

Spotting in Early Pregnancy: What It Means?

Spotting means seeing a few drops or small streaks of blood on your underwear or when you wipe after using the toilet. It may be pink, brown or red and can happen during the first trimester.

Light spotting is fairly common in early pregnancy. Sometimes the cause is harmless, such as changes in the cervix. In other cases, it may be related to a pregnancy complication.

So, even if it's only a few spots and you feel perfectly fine, let your gynaecologist know. A little bleeding doesn't automatically mean something is wrong, but it's always worth checking.

Common Causes of Spotting in the First Trimester

There are several reasons why you may notice spotting during early pregnancy.

  • Implantation: Light bleeding may occur around the time the fertilised egg attaches to the lining of the uterus.
  • Cervical changes: Pregnancy increases blood flow to the cervix, making it more sensitive and likely to bleed.
  • After intercourse or an examination: The sensitive cervix may bleed slightly after sex or an internal examination.
  • Hormonal changes: Some women experience light spotting during early pregnancy.
  • Infections: Cervical or vaginal infections can sometimes cause bleeding.
  • Pregnancy complications: Spotting can also occur with miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.

Sometimes, even after an examination, the exact cause of spotting may not be identified.

Implantation Bleeding: A Possible Early Cause

Implantation happens when the fertilised egg attaches to the lining of the uterus. Some women notice very light spotting around this time, often close to when their period is due. It may appear as a few pink or brown spots and usually doesn't resemble a regular menstrual flow. But here's something important: you cannot confirm implantation bleeding just by looking at its colour or amount. Other causes of early pregnancy bleeding can look similar. It’s not necessary to have implantation bleeding in all pregnancies. If you've already had a positive pregnancy test and notice spotting, don't automatically assume it's implantation bleeding. Inform your doctor.

Spotting vs Period: Knowing the Difference

Spotting is usually much lighter than a period. You may notice only a few drops on your underwear or toilet paper, without needing a sanitary pad.

A period generally has a more regular flow, often becoming heavier over the first few days.

During pregnancy, however, bleeding can sometimes be more than just spotting. If you're already pregnant, don't assume bleeding is your period or try to judge its cause by how it looks.

A pregnancy test confirms pregnancy, but it cannot tell you why you're bleeding.

Brown, Pink or Red Spotting: Does Colour Matter?

You may notice different colours of blood during early pregnancy:

  • Brown: Often represents older blood that has taken longer to come out.
  • Pink: May be a small amount of blood mixed with vaginal discharge.
  • Red: Usually indicates fresher blood.

While these differences can help describe what you're seeing, colour alone cannot tell you whether the bleeding is harmless or serious.

Pay attention to the amount of bleeding, whether it's increasing and whether you have pain, cramps or dizziness. Your doctor will consider all these details when assessing you.

Spotting and Miscarriage: Understanding the Connection

Yes, spotting or bleeding can sometimes be a sign of miscarriage, especially when accompanied by cramping, heavier bleeding or passing clots or tissue.

But please remember: bleeding does not always mean miscarriage. Many women experience spotting in the first trimester and continue to have healthy pregnancies. If you notice bleeding, your doctor may recommend an ultrasound to check the pregnancy. Depending on how early you are, blood tests measuring hCG may also be needed. Sometimes repeat scans or blood tests are required before a clear answer is available. Don't jump to conclusions based on bleeding alone.

Ectopic Pregnancy: Warning Signs You Must Not Ignore

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilised egg implants outside the uterus, most commonly in a fallopian tube. It cannot develop normally and can become dangerous if not treated in time.

Spotting or vaginal bleeding may be one of its early symptoms.

Watch out for these warning signs:

  • Persistent pain in the lower abdomen, especially on one side.
  • Vaginal spotting or bleeding along with abdominal pain.
  • Pain at the tip of your shoulder.
  • Dizziness, weakness or fainting.
  • Sudden or severe abdominal pain.

If you experience severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, fainting or heavy bleeding, go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

An ectopic pregnancy needs prompt medical assessment, even if you haven't yet had your first pregnancy scan.

How Much Bleeding Needs Medical Attention?

A few spots may seem minor, but the amount of blood alone cannot tell you whether everything is fine.

As a general guide:

  • A few spots: Inform your gynaecologist and follow their advice.
  • Bleeding that continues or increases: Contact your doctor promptly for assessment.
  • Bleeding that soaks a pad, passing clots or tissue, or bleeding with significant pain: Seek urgent medical attention.
  • Heavy bleeding with severe pain, dizziness or fainting: Go to the emergency department immediately.

Don't wait for bleeding to become heavy before seeking advice.

When to Contact Your Gynaecologist?

If you notice any spotting or bleeding after a positive pregnancy test, contact your gynaecologist for guidance, even if it has stopped.

Your doctor may ask you about:

  • How many weeks pregnant you are.
  • When the spotting started and how long it lasted.
  • The amount and appearance of the blood.
  • Whether you have cramps, abdominal pain or dizziness.
  • Your previous pregnancy history.

Depending on your symptoms and pregnancy stage, you may need an ultrasound, blood tests or other investigations.

If you know that your blood group is Rh-negative, mention this to your doctor, as they can advise whether any additional treatment is needed.

Spotting After Sex or an Internal Examination

Noticed a little blood after intercourse or an internal examination? This can happen during pregnancy.

The cervix receives increased blood supply during pregnancy and becomes more sensitive. Even gentle contact may sometimes cause light spotting.

It usually settles, but inform your doctor, particularly if the bleeding continues, increases or is accompanied by pain.

Bed Rest and Activity After Spotting

You may have heard that you should stay in bed if you experience spotting during pregnancy. But strict bed rest is not routinely recommended to prevent miscarriage, as there is no good evidence that it prevents pregnancy loss.

Your doctor may suggest temporary changes to your activities depending on the cause of bleeding and your individual condition.

Avoid starting medicines, stopping prescribed medicines or putting yourself on strict bed rest without medical advice. Follow the plan recommended by your gynaecologist.

Tracking Your Spotting and Other Symptoms

When you're worried, it can be difficult to remember exactly when the spotting started or how much bleeding you noticed.

Keep a small record of:

  • Date and time of spotting.
  • Colour and approximate amount of blood.
  • Whether it was occasional or continuous.
  • Any cramps, abdominal pain or other symptoms.
  • Whether it happened after intercourse or an examination.

This information can help your doctor understand what happened and decide whether further assessment is needed.

You can use the MiGynae app to keep track of your pregnancy symptoms and important notes. Remember, tracking is helpful, but it should never delay medical attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Is light spotting in early pregnancy normal?

Light spotting is fairly common in early pregnancy, and many women go on to have healthy pregnancies. However, any bleeding should be discussed with your gynaecologist to rule out possible complications.

2. How do I identify implantation bleeding?

Implantation-related spotting may appear as a few light pink or brown spots around the time your period is due. However, its appearance cannot confirm implantation or rule out other causes of bleeding.

3. Is brown discharge in early pregnancy dangerous?

Brown discharge often indicates older blood, but colour alone cannot establish whether it is harmless. Inform your doctor, especially if it persists, increases or is accompanied by pain.

4. Does spotting always mean miscarriage?

No. Spotting can happen for several reasons, and many women with early pregnancy bleeding continue to have healthy pregnancies. An examination and ultrasound may help identify the cause.

5. When is spotting an emergency during pregnancy?

Seek immediate medical attention if you have heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or fainting. These symptoms can indicate a serious complication, including ectopic pregnancy.

6. Should I take bed rest if I have spotting?

Strict bed rest has not been shown to prevent miscarriage. Follow your gynaecologist's advice about activity and rest based on your individual condition.

A final reminder: Spotting can be frightening, especially in the early weeks when you are still waiting for your first scan or heartbeat confirmation. Don't panic, but don't ignore it either. Get the right medical advice, watch for warning signs and give yourself the care and reassurance you need.

title: Stomach Cramps During Early Pregnancy: What's Normal and What's Not
excerpt: Experiencing mild twinges and lower abdominal cramping in early pregnancy? Learn why uterine stretching causes discomfort and how to recognize red flags.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Why Does the Abdomen Cramp in Early Pregnancy?

Mild menstrual-like dull aches and pulling sensations in the lower pelvis are surprisingly common during early gestation. Your uterus is undergoing rapid hormonal and physical changes to prepare a safe haven for your growing baby.

Normal Physiological Causes

  • Implantation & Hormonal Surges: During weeks 4 to 6, hormonal shifts and implantation frequently produce mild twinges resembling pre-period aches.
  • Uterine Muscle Expansion: As the uterus begins growing from the size of a plum to a grapefruit, stretching muscle fibers and ligaments can cause intermittent dull aches.
  • Gas and Progesterone Bloating: Pregnancy progesterone slows gastrointestinal motility, leading to trapped gas and intestinal cramps that feel remarkably like uterine twinges.

Safe Home Relief Tips

To ease benign pregnancy cramping:

  • Rest with feet elevated and practice slow, diaphragmatic breathing.
  • Sip warm water or soothing chamomile or jeera water.
  • Avoid sudden twisting motions when rising from bed.
  • Never apply direct hot water bottles or heating pads to your abdomen during the first trimester.

Warning Signs Requiring Urgent Medical Evaluation

Seek prompt medical consultation if cramping is severe, worsening, strictly localized to one side of the pelvis, or accompanied by shoulder tip pain, vaginal bleeding, or fever.

title: Constipation During Pregnancy: Natural Remedies & Safe Relief
excerpt: Hormones and prenatal iron supplements can slow digestion. Here is an OBGYN-backed guide to relieving pregnancy constipation with safe Indian foods, fluids, and habits.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Understanding Pregnancy Constipation

Constipation affects nearly half of all women during pregnancy. High circulating levels of progesterone relax the smooth muscles throughout your body, including the digestive tract. This slows transit time, allowing the colon to absorb more water and leaving stools harder and more difficult to pass.

Key Contributing Factors

  • Progesterone Hormones: Slows peristaltic bowel contractions.
  • Prenatal Iron Supplements: Essential for preventing maternal anemia, but iron formulations can irritate and slow bowel movement.
  • Expanding Uterus: In the second and third trimesters, the anatomical weight of the uterus exerts physical pressure on the rectum.

Proven Indian Dietary Remedies

  • Hydration Priority: Drink 2.5 to 3 liters of water daily. Warm water upon waking stimulates the gastrocolic reflex.
  • High-Fiber Grains: Incorporate daliya (cracked wheat), oats, red rice, and jowar/bajra rotis into daily meals.
  • Natural Laxative Fruits: Ripe papaya (moderately in 2nd/3rd trimester under medical guidance), stewed prunes, pears, apples with peel, and soaked raisins.
  • Isabgol (Psyllium Husk): 1 teaspoon of Isabgol in a glass of warm water or milk at bedtime provides gentle, non-habit-forming bulk fiber (always check with your doctor first).

Never take over-the-counter chemical stimulant laxatives without consulting your OBGYN, as some can stimulate uterine irritability.

title: Acidity and Heartburn in Pregnancy: Causes and Indian Home Remedies
excerpt: Struggling with acid reflux and chest burning during pregnancy? Discover practical eating hacks, posture advice, and traditional Indian home remedies that work.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Why Does Acidity Spike During Pregnancy?

Heartburn and severe acid reflux are frequent complaints among Indian expectant mothers, especially from the late second trimester onwards. The culprit is twofold: progesterone relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter (the muscular valve preventing stomach acid from creeping up into the esophagus), and your growing baby physically pushes stomach contents upwards.

Effective Lifestyle Hacks to Prevent Reflux

  • Eat Smaller, Frequent Meals: Divide your daily nutrition into 5 to 6 small portions rather than 3 heavy meals. Overfilling the stomach exacerbates backflow.
  • Remain Upright After Eating: Avoid lying down for at least 60 to 90 minutes post-meal. A gentle 15-minute stroll indoors aids digestion.
  • Elevate Your Head at Night: Prop your head and upper torso up with an extra pillow or pregnancy wedge to use gravity against reflux.

Traditional, Safe Soothing Remedies

  • Cold Milk / Buttermilk: A few sips of chilled skim milk or fresh chaas (buttermilk) prepared with roasted cumin (jeera) neutralizes acute acid spikes.
  • Fennel Seeds (Saunf): Chewing half a teaspoon of plain roasted saunf after meals stimulates salivary enzymes and calms gastric irritation.
  • Coconut Water: A natural electrolyte drink that cools the digestive tract and hydrates without adding heavy acidity.

If severe reflux interferes with sleep or your ability to eat, consult your doctor. Safe antacid syrups and pregnancy-approved H2 blockers are readily available.

title: White Discharge During Pregnancy: What's Healthy and When to Worry
excerpt: Leukorrhea is an increase in normal vaginal discharge during pregnancy. Learn how to identify healthy discharge, prevent infections, and spot signs of yeast or bacterial vaginosis.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
What is Physiological Leukorrhea?

Noticeable increases in thin, milky-white, or clear vaginal discharge are completely normal and healthy during pregnancy. This discharge—termed leukorrhea—is driven by elevated estrogen levels and increased blood flow to the pelvic region. Its biological purpose is protective: it prevents bacteria from ascending into the uterus and cervix.

Characteristics of Normal, Healthy Discharge

  • Color: Clear, milky white, or creamy ivory
  • Consistency: Thin, mucus-like, or slightly stretchy
  • Odor: Mild, sweetish, or completely odorless

Signs of Vaginal Infection (Yeast or Bacterial Vaginosis)

Hormonal fluctuations alter vaginal pH, making expectant mothers more prone to candidiasis (yeast) and bacterial imbalances. Consult your doctor if your discharge exhibits:

  • Thick, clumpy, white texture resembling curd (paneer), accompanied by intense vulvar itching and redness (classic yeast infection)
  • Greyish-green or yellow frothy discharge with a strong, unpleasant fishy odor
  • Pain or burning sensations during urination or intimacy

Hygiene Tips for Expecting Mothers

Wear breathable cotton underwear, change undergarments if damp, avoid synthetic tight pants, and never use scented chemical intimate washes or douches. Warm water is best for daily external cleansing.

content:
Being told you have high blood sugar during pregnancy can be worrying. You may immediately wonder whether your baby is safe, whether you will need insulin injections and, most importantly, what you can eat now!

First, take a breath. Gestational diabetes (GDM) is quite common during pregnancy and can usually be managed with the right diet, activity and medical care. It is not your fault, and it does not mean you have to give up all your favourite foods.

Let's understand why it happens, when you need testing and how you can manage it while still enjoying a balanced Indian diet.

Understanding Gestational Diabetes: Why It Happens During Pregnancy

Gestational diabetes is a condition in which blood sugar levels become higher than normal during pregnancy.

During pregnancy, your body produces hormones that make it harder for insulin to work effectively. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from your blood into your body's cells, where it is used for energy.

Normally, your pancreas produces extra insulin to manage this change. But sometimes, it cannot produce enough to meet the increased demand. As a result, sugar starts building up in your blood.

This is called gestational diabetes.

One important thing to remember: GDM is not simply caused by eating too much sugar. Pregnancy-related hormonal changes play a major role, and even women who eat healthy and stay active can develop it.

Symptoms of Gestational Diabetes: Why You May Not Notice Anything

Most women with gestational diabetes do not experience any noticeable symptoms. You may feel perfectly normal even when your blood sugar levels are high.

Some women may notice:

  • Increased thirst.
  • Passing urine more frequently.
  • Unusual tiredness.
  • Blurred vision.
  • Recurrent urinary or vaginal infections.

But these symptoms can also occur in an otherwise normal pregnancy.

That's why you cannot identify gestational diabetes just by how you feel. A blood sugar screening test is the only reliable way to detect it.

Risk Factors: Who Is More Likely to Develop GDM?

Gestational diabetes can happen to any pregnant woman, but certain factors may increase your chances.

You may have a higher risk if you:

  • Are overweight or obese.
  • Have a family history of diabetes, especially in parents or siblings.
  • Have PCOS.
  • Had gestational diabetes in an earlier pregnancy.
  • Previously delivered a baby with a high birth weight.
  • Have a history of prediabetes or elevated blood sugar.

However, having none of these risk factors does not mean you cannot develop GDM.

Since gestational diabetes is relatively common in India, screening is recommended broadly rather than only for women considered high-risk.

GTT During Pregnancy: When and How the Test Is Done

The Glucose Tolerance Test (GTT), also called the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), checks how your body handles sugar.

In India, many clinics follow the DIPSI method, which is convenient because it does not require fasting.

Your doctor may recommend testing:

  • At your first antenatal visit.
  • Again around 24–28 weeks if your initial test is normal.
  • Later in pregnancy if you have additional risk factors or a medical reason for repeat testing.

Don't miss the test just because you feel healthy. GDM often develops without symptoms.

DIPSI Test in India: Do You Need to Fast?

DIPSI stands for Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group of India. It is a commonly used testing method in Indian antenatal care.

Here's how it works:

  • You are given a drink containing 75 grams of glucose.
  • You do not need to fast before drinking it.
  • Your blood sample is taken two hours after consuming the glucose drink.

The blood sugar result is used to assess whether you have gestational diabetes. Under the DIPSI criteria, a two-hour blood glucose value of 140 mg/dL or higher is used to diagnose GDM.

Some hospitals may follow a different OGTT protocol, such as a fasting test with additional blood samples. So always confirm whether your test requires fasting and follow the instructions given by your hospital.

Understanding Your GTT Report: What Do the Numbers Mean?

You may come across different blood sugar cutoffs when searching online. That's because different testing methods use different criteria.

For example, DIPSI uses the two-hour value after a 75-gram glucose drink, whereas other protocols measure fasting, one-hour and two-hour blood sugar levels.

This is why you should not compare your result with a random number found online.

Ask your doctor:

  • Which testing method was used?
  • Is my result normal or above the recommended range?
  • Do I need repeat testing or further monitoring?

Your doctor will interpret the result using the correct criteria for your test and decide what needs to be done next.

Diagnosed with Gestational Diabetes: What Happens Next?

First, don't panic. A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean you will need insulin or a Caesarean delivery.

Your doctor will usually recommend a few changes to help bring your blood sugar levels under control. These may include:

  • A personalised meal plan.
  • Regular blood sugar monitoring.
  • Walking or other suitable physical activity.
  • More frequent antenatal check-ups.
  • Medication, if needed.

Many women achieve good sugar control with nutrition and physical activity alone. If your readings remain above your doctor's targets, medicines may be added.

The aim is to keep your blood sugar within the recommended range throughout pregnancy.

Indian Diet for Gestational Diabetes: What Should You Eat?

You do not need to stop eating carbohydrates completely. Your body and your growing baby still need adequate nutrition.

The key is to choose better carbohydrate sources, watch your portions and combine them with protein and fibre. A few simple guidelines can help:

  • Eat regular meals: Avoid skipping meals or going for long periods without eating.
  • Add protein: Include dal, chana, rajma, paneer, curd, tofu, eggs or other suitable protein sources.
  • Choose fibre-rich foods: Include vegetables, whole fruits, oats, whole grains and pulses.
  • Watch your portions: Even healthy foods can raise blood sugar if eaten in excessive quantities.
  • Avoid sugary drinks: Replace packaged juices, soft drinks and sweetened beverages with water, unsweetened chaas or other suitable drinks.
  • Spread your carbohydrates: Divide your food across three meals and two or three small snacks, as advised by your dietitian.

A simple way to plan your plate is to fill half with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with protein-rich foods and the remaining quarter with roti, rice or another carbohydrate source.

Your exact portions should be adjusted according to your nutritional needs and blood sugar readings.

Rice and Roti in Gestational Diabetes: What Can You Eat?

This is probably one of the biggest worries after a GDM diagnosis! The good news is that you do not have to completely stop eating rice or roti.

You can include both in your diet, but portion size and how you combine them matter. Some practical choices:

  • Choose whole-wheat roti or try millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi.
  • Include measured portions of rice rather than large servings.
  • Combine roti or rice with dal, vegetables, curd, paneer or tofu.
  • Avoid eating a large portion of rice or roti without protein and vegetables.
  • Check your post-meal sugar readings to understand how your body responds.

Remember, switching to brown rice or millets does not automatically make a meal suitable for GDM. Portion size and your individual blood sugar response matter too.

Fruits and Snacks: Making Better Everyday Choices

You don't have to stop eating fruits just because you have gestational diabetes. Choose whole fruits rather than fruit juices, and pay attention to portion sizes.

Some convenient snack ideas include:

  • A small serving of guava, apple, pear or orange.
  • Roasted chana.
  • A handful of unsalted nuts.
  • Plain curd.
  • Vegetable sticks with hummus.
  • A small portion of sprouts, cooked safely.

Try pairing fruit with a protein or healthy-fat source when suitable. Your dietitian can help decide the right portions and timing. Avoid replacing whole fruits with packaged fruit juices, which can deliver a large amount of sugar without the same fibre.

Festivals, Sweets and Gestational Diabetes

Having GDM does not mean you have to feel left out at every family celebration. However, sweets and desserts can raise your blood sugar quickly, so portion control is important.

A few practical tips:

  • Avoid eating sweets on an empty stomach.
  • If your doctor or dietitian permits, enjoy a small portion occasionally.
  • Avoid combining several sweet dishes in one meal.
  • Keep your regular meals balanced.
  • Check your blood sugar as advised.

You may need to adjust your meal plan around celebrations, so discuss this with your dietitian rather than making changes to your medicines or skipping meals.

Insulin During Pregnancy: Is It Necessary and Is It Safe?

Not every woman with gestational diabetes needs insulin. Your doctor may first recommend dietary changes, physical activity and regular sugar monitoring. If your blood sugar remains above the target range despite these measures, medication may be needed.

Insulin is a well-established and commonly preferred treatment for gestational diabetes when medication is required. It does not cross the placenta in significant amounts.

In some situations, your doctor may also discuss metformin after considering its benefits and limitations.

Needing insulin does not mean you failed to control your sugar through diet. Pregnancy hormones can increase insulin resistance, and sometimes your body simply needs additional support. Never start, stop or adjust diabetes medication without your doctor's advice.

How Gestational Diabetes Can Affect Your Baby and Pregnancy

When blood sugar remains high during pregnancy, it can increase the risk of certain complications. These may include:

  • Your baby growing larger than expected.
  • Increased chances of difficult vaginal delivery or birth injuries.
  • High blood pressure and pre-eclampsia in the mother.
  • Low blood sugar in the newborn after birth.
  • The baby needing additional observation after delivery.

The good news is that timely diagnosis, regular monitoring and proper treatment can significantly reduce these risks. Your doctor may recommend additional growth scans or fetal monitoring depending on your blood sugar control and other pregnancy-related factors.

After Delivery: Does Gestational Diabetes Go Away?

For most women, blood sugar levels return to normal after childbirth because the pregnancy-related hormonal changes begin to settle.

However, having gestational diabetes means you have a higher chance of developing type 2 diabetes in the future. That's why follow-up testing is important even if you feel completely fine after childbirth.

Your doctor will usually recommend:

  • A postpartum blood sugar test, commonly around 6–12 weeks after delivery.
  • Further diabetes screening at regular intervals.
  • Healthy eating and physical activity.
  • Blood sugar testing before planning your next pregnancy.

Do not skip your postpartum test. It is an important part of looking after your long-term health.

A final reminder: Gestational diabetes can feel overwhelming at first, especially when you start worrying about every meal. But you don't have to figure it all out alone. With the right diet, regular monitoring and guidance from your doctor, you can manage your blood sugar and have a healthy pregnancy.

title: Low Haemoglobin and Anemia in Pregnancy: Causes, Diet & Iron Therapy
excerpt: Maternal anemia affects over 50% of Indian pregnancies. Understand the symptoms of low iron, target haemoglobin levels, iron-rich foods, and preventing fatigue.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Understanding Pregnancy Anemia

During pregnancy, your total blood volume expands by nearly 50% to supply oxygen and nutrients to your developing placenta and fetus. While plasma volume increases dramatically, red blood cell production must catch up—a physiological phenomenon called hemodilution.

Target Haemoglobin (Hb) Levels

The World Health Organization (WHO) and Ministry of Health define anemia in pregnancy as an Hb below 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, or below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester.

Common Symptoms of Anemia

  • Persistent, unrefreshing fatigue and weakness
  • Pale skin, lips, or inner eyelids
  • Shortness of breath with minimal exertion
  • Rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations)
  • Cold extremities and occasional dizziness

Iron-Rich Indian Nutrition

  • Vegetarian Sources: Spinach (palak), methi, beetroot, lentils (masoor/moong), jaggery (gud in moderation), dates, raisins, and roasted chana.
  • Non-Vegetarian Sources: Well-cooked eggs and poultry provide highly bioavailable heme iron.
  • The Vitamin C Synergy: Iron absorption is significantly amplified when paired with vitamin C. Squeeze fresh lemon juice over your dal or enjoy an amla (Indian gooseberry) with meals.
  • Avoid Calcium Blockers: Do not consume milk, tea, or coffee within 2 hours of taking your iron supplement, as calcium and tannins inhibit iron absorption.

Your first pregnancy scan, the NT scan, the detailed anomaly scan… there seem to be so many scans to remember during pregnancy! And each time your doctor writes a new scan on your prescription, you may wonder what it is for and whether everything is okay.

The good thing is that every scan has a specific purpose. Some confirm your pregnancy and due date, some check your baby's development, while others help monitor growth and blood flow later in pregnancy.

Let's go through the important pregnancy scans, when they are usually done and what you can expect at each stage.

Number of Ultrasound Scans During a Normal Pregnancy

There isn't one fixed number of ultrasound scans that every pregnant woman needs. It depends on your pregnancy, medical history and your doctor's assessment.

Your doctor may recommend:

  • An early pregnancy or dating scan, if needed.
  • An NT scan during the first trimester.
  • A detailed anomaly scan in the second trimester.
  • A growth scan in the third trimester, if advised.
  • Additional scans or Doppler studies if there is a medical reason.

Some women may need more scans to monitor specific concerns, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, twins or slow fetal growth. This does not automatically mean something is wrong.

The aim is not to have as many scans as possible, but to have the right scans at the right time.

First Pregnancy Scan: Dating and Viability Scan

Usually around 6–10 weeks, when an early scan is needed

This is often the first ultrasound during pregnancy. It helps confirm that the pregnancy is inside the uterus and checks whether the baby is developing as expected for that stage.

Your doctor may use this scan to:

  • Confirm the location of the pregnancy.
  • Check for a heartbeat, depending on how early the scan is done.
  • Estimate your pregnancy week and expected due date.
  • Check whether you are carrying one baby or twins.

If your periods are irregular or you are unsure about your last menstrual period date, an early scan can be particularly helpful in estimating your due date.

Don't worry if the scan is done very early and everything cannot be seen clearly. Sometimes a repeat scan after a few days is needed.

NT Scan and First-Trimester Screening

11 weeks to 13 weeks and 6 days

The NT (nuchal translucency) scan is an important first-trimester screening scan. It measures a small fluid-filled space at the back of your baby's neck.

Along with your age and other screening information, this measurement helps estimate the chance of certain chromosomal conditions, including Down syndrome.

Your doctor may also recommend a blood test called the Double Marker test along with the NT scan.

A few things to remember:

  • The NT scan is a screening test, not a diagnostic test.
  • A higher-risk result does not confirm that your baby has a chromosomal condition.
  • Your doctor may discuss further screening, such as NIPT, or diagnostic testing if needed.

Try not to miss this scan window, as the measurement is useful only during a specific stage of pregnancy.

Anomaly Scan (Level II or TIFFA): The Detailed Baby Scan

Usually between 18 and 22 weeks

This is one of the most important scans of pregnancy. Also called the Level II or TIFFA scan, it gives a detailed look at your baby's developing organs and body structures.

The doctor or sonologist examines:

  • Brain and skull.
  • Face and spine.
  • Heart and chest.
  • Stomach, kidneys and bladder.
  • Arms, legs, hands and feet.
  • Placenta and amniotic fluid.
  • Cervix, when indicated.

The scan helps identify many major structural abnormalities and checks whether your baby's organs are developing as expected.

It may take longer than your earlier scans because several structures need to be examined carefully. Sometimes the baby is not in the right position, and you may be asked to walk around or return for a few additional images.

Remember, even a normal anomaly scan cannot detect every possible birth defect or health condition.

Fetal Echocardiography: A Closer Look at Your Baby's Heart

Usually around 18–24 weeks, when indicated

A fetal echo is a specialised ultrasound that examines your baby's heart in greater detail. It looks at the heart's structure, chambers, valves and blood flow.

It is not routinely needed in every pregnancy. Your doctor may recommend it if:

  • A possible heart abnormality is seen during the anomaly scan.
  • You have certain medical conditions, such as diabetes present before pregnancy.
  • There is a close family history of congenital heart disease.
  • Your baby has certain scan findings that need further assessment.

Being advised to get a fetal echo does not mean your baby definitely has a heart problem. It simply allows the specialist to examine the heart more closely.

Third-Trimester Growth Scan

Usually between 32 and 36 weeks, if advised

As your baby grows, your doctor may recommend a growth scan to check whether the baby is growing as expected.

This scan usually assesses:

  • Estimated fetal weight and measurements.
  • Baby's growth in relation to the pregnancy week.
  • Amniotic fluid levels.
  • Placental position.
  • Baby's position in the uterus.

It is particularly useful when there are concerns about slow or excessive growth, high blood pressure, diabetes or other pregnancy-related conditions.

The timing may be different depending on your medical history and the reason for the scan.

Doppler Scan: Checking Blood Flow to Your Baby

A Doppler scan is used to assess blood flow through selected blood vessels, such as those in the umbilical cord and baby's circulation. It helps your doctor understand how well blood is flowing between the placenta and baby.

Your doctor may recommend it if:

  • Your baby is measuring smaller than expected.
  • There is a concern about fetal growth restriction (FGR).
  • You have high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia.
  • There is a concern about placental function.

Doppler is not required in every uncomplicated pregnancy. It is usually advised when your doctor needs additional information about your baby's circulation and wellbeing.

It may be performed along with a growth scan or as a separate examination.

Pregnancy Ultrasound Costs in India and Free Scan Options

The cost of pregnancy scans varies depending on the city, hospital, diagnostic centre and type of scan.

A detailed anomaly scan may cost a few thousand rupees at a private centre, while specialised scans such as fetal echo or Doppler may have separate charges.

Before booking, ask the centre about the total cost, whether the report is included and whether any additional assessment may be charged separately.

Free ultrasound services under PMSMA

The Government of India's Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) provides free antenatal care on the 9th of every month at designated government health facilities. Services include antenatal check-ups, investigations and ultrasound facilities.

You can contact your nearest government health centre to check availability and the process for getting a scan.

Ultrasound Safety During Pregnancy

One common worry among expectant mothers is whether repeated ultrasound scans can harm the baby.

Ultrasound uses sound waves, not X-rays or radiation. Diagnostic ultrasound has a well-established safety record when performed by trained professionals for appropriate medical reasons.

However, this doesn't mean you need extra scans without a medical reason.

Follow your doctor's recommended schedule, get your scans done at an appropriate centre and avoid unnecessary scans just for photographs or videos of the baby.

When Scan Dates Differ from Your Last Period

Sometimes your ultrasound report may show a pregnancy age or due date that is slightly different from the date calculated using your last menstrual period (LMP).

This can happen because:

  • You may have ovulated later than expected.
  • Your menstrual cycles may be irregular.
  • You may not remember the exact date of your last period.

An early ultrasound, particularly one measuring the baby's crown-rump length (CRL), is a reliable way to establish pregnancy dates.

Once your doctor has confirmed your expected due date using an appropriate early scan, later growth scans are generally used to assess your baby's growth rather than repeatedly changing the due date.

A little reminder: Keep all your ultrasound reports safely and carry them to every antenatal visit. Each report helps your doctor understand how your pregnancy is progressing and plan the care you need.

Once your pregnancy is confirmed, your doctor will recommend a series of blood tests, urine tests and scans at different stages. You may wonder why so many tests are needed when you are feeling perfectly fine!

The reason is simple: different tests help check different aspects of your health and your baby's development. Some are done only once, while others need to be repeated as pregnancy progresses.

To make things easier, here's a trimester-wise checklist of the important pregnancy tests commonly recommended in India, what they check and when you may need them.

First Trimester Tests (Weeks 1–12): Your Initial Pregnancy Check-up

Your first antenatal visit is ideally scheduled before 12 weeks. This is when your doctor gets a complete picture of your health and checks for conditions that may need attention during pregnancy.

1. Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Haemoglobin

This blood test checks your haemoglobin, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

It helps identify:

  • Anaemia (low haemoglobin).
  • Low platelet counts.
  • Other abnormalities in your blood count that may need further evaluation.

Anaemia is common during pregnancy, so checking your haemoglobin early helps your doctor decide whether you need iron supplementation or further tests.

2. Blood Group, Rh Factor and Antibody Screening

Your blood group (A, B, AB or O) and Rh status (positive or negative) are checked early in pregnancy.

If you are Rh-negative, your doctor may also check for antibodies that could affect your baby's red blood cells.

Knowing your blood group early helps your doctor plan the right precautions and treatment if needed.

3. Infection Screening: HIV, Hepatitis B and Syphilis

These tests screen for infections that can sometimes pass from mother to baby during pregnancy or childbirth.

Early detection is important because appropriate treatment and precautions can greatly reduce the risk of transmission.

Your doctor may also recommend screening for other infections depending on your medical history and local guidelines.

4. Thyroid Test (TSH)

Thyroid hormones play an important role in your baby's growth and development, especially during early pregnancy.

A TSH blood test helps check whether your thyroid is functioning properly.

If you already have thyroid problems or your result is abnormal, your doctor may recommend additional thyroid tests and repeat monitoring during pregnancy.

5. Blood Sugar Test (DIPSI)

In India, the DIPSI test is commonly used to screen for gestational diabetes.

You are given a drink containing 75 grams of glucose, and your blood sugar is checked two hours later. Unlike some other glucose tolerance tests, the DIPSI method does not require fasting.

Even if you have no symptoms or family history of diabetes, your doctor may recommend this test at your first antenatal visit.

If the result is normal, it is generally repeated after 24 weeks as advised by your doctor.

6. Urine Routine Examination and Urine Culture

A urine test helps check for:

  • Protein, which may need further assessment.
  • Sugar in the urine.
  • Pus cells or other signs of infection.

Your doctor may also recommend a urine culture to detect bacteria, even when you have no burning or urinary symptoms. This is important because an untreated urinary infection during pregnancy can sometimes cause complications.

7. Additional Screening for Thalassemia and Other Blood Disorders

Depending on your family history, blood count and regional risk, your doctor may recommend screening for thalassemia or sickle cell disease.

These tests help identify inherited blood conditions that may be passed on to the baby. If you are found to be a carrier, your partner may also need testing.

8. NT Scan and Double Marker Test

Usually between 11 weeks and 13 weeks 6 days

These are first-trimester screening tests used to estimate the risk of certain chromosomal conditions, including Down syndrome.

The NT scan measures a small fluid-filled space at the back of your baby's neck. The Double Marker is a blood test that measures two pregnancy-related proteins.

Together with other factors, these results help calculate your baby's screening risk.

Remember, these are screening tests, not diagnostic tests. A higher-risk result does not mean your baby definitely has a chromosomal condition.

For a detailed explanation, read our guide on Pregnancy Scans in India.

Second Trimester Tests (Weeks 13–26): Checking Your Baby's Development

The second trimester is an important time for checking your baby's organ development and screening for conditions that may develop as pregnancy progresses.

1. Quadruple Marker Test (If First-Trimester Screening Was Missed)

Usually between 14 and 20 weeks

If you missed the NT and Double Marker screening window, your doctor may offer a Quadruple Marker blood test.

It measures four substances in your blood to estimate the risk of certain chromosomal conditions and neural tube defects.

It is important to understand that this is also a screening test, not a diagnosis.

2. Anomaly Scan (Level II or TIFFA)

Usually between 18 and 22 weeks

This is a detailed ultrasound that checks your baby's developing organs and body structures, including the brain, heart, spine, kidneys, limbs and other important structures.

It also helps assess the placenta and amniotic fluid.

This scan is one of the most important pregnancy milestones, so make sure you book it within the recommended window.

3. Glucose Tolerance Test (GTT)

Usually repeated after 24 weeks if earlier screening was normal

Your doctor may repeat the glucose test to check for gestational diabetes, even if your earlier result was normal.

Pregnancy hormones can increase insulin resistance as pregnancy progresses, which is why a repeat test is important.

The method may be DIPSI or another glucose tolerance protocol, depending on your hospital.

4. Repeat Haemoglobin Test

Your doctor may repeat your haemoglobin or complete blood count around 24–28 weeks to check for anaemia.

Your baby's growth and the increase in your blood volume can make anaemia more likely as pregnancy progresses.

If your haemoglobin is low, your doctor may adjust your iron treatment or recommend additional investigations.

5. Repeat Urine Examination

Urine testing continues during antenatal visits to check for protein and other abnormalities.

A repeat urine examination or culture may also be recommended around this stage, particularly if you have a history of urinary infections or an earlier abnormal result.

6. Rh Antibody Screening and Anti-D Planning

If you have an Rh-negative blood group, your doctor may repeat your antibody screening around 28 weeks.

If you are Rh-negative and have not already developed anti-D antibodies, your doctor will discuss Anti-D injection, commonly given around 28 weeks, to prevent Rh sensitisation.

The injection is also considered after certain bleeding episodes or procedures, depending on the stage of pregnancy.

Third Trimester Tests (Weeks 27–40): Preparing for Delivery

As you enter the final months, the focus shifts towards your baby's growth, your health and preparing for childbirth.

1. Repeat Haemoglobin Test

A further haemoglobin check may be recommended around 36–40 weeks to make sure your levels are adequate before delivery.

This is particularly important if you had anaemia earlier in pregnancy or needed iron treatment.

2. Blood Pressure and Urine Protein Checks

At your antenatal visits, your doctor will continue checking your blood pressure and urine for protein.

These checks help identify conditions such as pregnancy-induced hypertension and pre-eclampsia, which may develop even if your earlier readings were normal.

Do not skip these routine checks just because you are feeling well.

3. Growth Scan and Doppler (If Advised)

Your doctor may recommend a third-trimester ultrasound to check:

  • Your baby's estimated weight and growth.
  • Amniotic fluid levels.
  • Placental position.
  • Your baby's position.

A Doppler scan may also be recommended if there are concerns about fetal growth or placental blood flow.

Not every woman needs a growth scan or Doppler at the same time. Your doctor will decide based on your pregnancy and previous findings.

4. Repeat Urine Tests or Other Investigations

If you have urinary symptoms, previous abnormal urine reports, high blood pressure or other medical concerns, your doctor may recommend additional urine or blood tests.

These are planned according to your individual needs rather than being compulsory for every pregnancy.

5. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) Screening, Where Recommended

Some hospitals and clinical protocols recommend a vaginal and rectal swab around 35–37 weeks to check for Group B Streptococcus (GBS).

GBS is a bacterium that can be present without causing symptoms but may occasionally cause infection in a newborn during delivery.

Screening and prevention practices vary between countries and hospitals in India. Ask your doctor whether this test is part of your hospital's protocol.

Anti-D Injection During Pregnancy: Who Needs It?

If your blood group is Rh-negative, Anti-D is an important part of pregnancy care when you have not already developed anti-D antibodies.

Your doctor will generally:

  • Check your blood group and Rh status early in pregnancy.
  • Screen for Rh antibodies.
  • Recommend routine Anti-D prophylaxis around 28 weeks when indicated.
  • Advise an additional dose after certain sensitising events, such as bleeding or an invasive procedure.
  • Check your baby's blood group after delivery and advise postpartum Anti-D if required.

Anti-D helps prevent your body from developing antibodies that could affect a future Rh-positive pregnancy.

If you are Rh-negative, make sure your gynaecologist knows about it from your first visit.

How Often Do You Need Antenatal Check-ups?

Pregnancy tests are only one part of antenatal care. Regular check-ups are equally important because some conditions can develop between scheduled tests.

For an uncomplicated pregnancy, a commonly recommended schedule is:

  • Up to 28 weeks: Approximately once a month.
  • 28–36 weeks: Every two weeks.
  • After 36 weeks: Usually once a week until delivery.

At these visits, your doctor may check your blood pressure, weight, urine protein, baby's growth and heartbeat, and discuss any symptoms or concerns.

High-risk pregnancies may need more frequent appointments and additional investigations.

Free Pregnancy Tests and Check-ups Under Government Schemes in India

If you are receiving antenatal care at a government health facility, you may be eligible for free investigations and ultrasound services.

Under the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (PMSMA), free antenatal check-ups are provided at designated government health facilities on the 9th of every month, particularly for women in their second and third trimesters.

The service package may include:

  • Doctor or specialist consultation.
  • Essential blood and urine investigations.
  • Ultrasound services.
  • Pregnancy risk assessment and counselling.

The exact services available can vary by facility. Contact your nearest government health centre to find out where and how to access them.

What If a Pregnancy Test Report Is Abnormal?

Seeing a result marked 'high', 'low' or 'abnormal' can be frightening, especially when you are pregnant.

But remember, an abnormal result does not always mean something is seriously wrong.

Sometimes your doctor may simply recommend:

  • Repeating the test.
  • Doing a more specific investigation.
  • Getting a specialist opinion.
  • Monitoring the result more frequently.

Don't compare your report with someone else's or try to interpret every value on your own. The meaning of a result depends on your pregnancy week, medical history and other findings.

Always review your reports with your gynaecologist.

A little reminder: Keep a folder of all your blood reports, urine tests and ultrasound scans. Carry it to every antenatal appointment so your doctor can follow your pregnancy journey easily.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What are the most important blood tests in the first trimester?

Common first-visit tests include CBC or haemoglobin, blood group and Rh factor, HIV, Hepatitis B, syphilis, thyroid (TSH), blood sugar screening and urine examination. Additional tests may be advised depending on your history.

2. Do all pregnancy blood tests require fasting?

No. Tests such as CBC, blood group, HIV and thyroid testing generally do not require fasting. The DIPSI glucose test also does not require fasting, but other glucose tolerance protocols may. Always confirm with your laboratory.

3. When is the GTT test done during pregnancy?

GDM screening is offered at the first antenatal visit under FOGSI guidance and repeated after 24 weeks if the initial result is normal. The exact timing and method may vary according to your doctor's protocol.

4. Can a CBC test confirm pregnancy?

No. A CBC checks your blood count and helps detect anaemia and other abnormalities. Pregnancy is confirmed through an hCG test in urine or blood.

5. What happens if I miss my NT scan?

If you miss the NT screening window, speak to your gynaecologist about other available screening options, such as the Quadruple Marker test or NIPT, depending on your pregnancy week and circumstances.

6. Are pregnancy tests free in India?

Eligible antenatal investigations and ultrasound services may be available free at designated government facilities under PMSMA. Ask your nearest government health centre about the services offered.

7. Do I need to repeat my blood tests in every trimester?

Some tests, such as haemoglobin screening and urine checks, may be repeated during pregnancy. Others, such as blood group testing, are usually done at the first visit, with antibody screening repeated when indicated. Your doctor will decide the repeat tests based on your reports and medical history.

Your pregnancy checklist is not meant to overwhelm you. Each test has a purpose, and knowing what to expect can make your antenatal visits much easier. Keep your appointments, save your reports and ask your doctor whenever something is unclear. A well-informed mother is better prepared for every stage of pregnancy.

title: Travelling During Pregnancy: Safe Flying, Car Trips & India Train Travel
excerpt: Planning a journey during pregnancy? Expert tips on the best trimester to travel, airline medical fit-to-fly certificates, car seatbelt safety, and staying comfortable.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Is it Safe to Travel While Pregnant?

In an uncomplicated, healthy pregnancy, travel is generally very safe when planned thoughtfully. The golden window for travel is the second trimester (weeks 14 to 28), when early morning sickness has subsided and energy levels are high, while the physical bulk of the third trimester has not yet peaked.

Air Travel Guidelines

  • Airline Policies: Most commercial Indian airlines (such as IndiGo and Air India) allow unrestricted flying up to week 28. Between weeks 28 and 36, a medical certificate (Fit to Fly) from your obstetrician is mandatory. Flying is typically prohibited after 36 weeks.
  • Hydration and Circulation: Cabin air is exceptionally dry. Sip water constantly and perform simple calf flexes every 30 minutes to reduce the risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).
  • Wear Compression Socks: Graduated knee-high compression stockings reduce ankle swelling during flights exceeding 2 hours.

Car and Road Travel Precautions

  • Proper Seatbelt Placement: Never position the lap belt across your pregnant belly. Place the lower strap low across your hips and pelvic bone, beneath your bump. The diagonal shoulder strap should rest securely across your chest between your breasts.
  • Frequent Breaks: On highway drives, pause every 90 minutes to stretch, walk, and use clean restroom facilities.
  • Avoid Rough Roads: Excessive jerking on unpaved or potholed roads can provoke abdominal discomfort or uterine contractions.

Train Travel Across India

Train travel offers ample room to recline and walk. Request lower berths in AC coaches, carry clean bottled water, pack home-prepared meals to avoid gastrointestinal infections, and travel accompanied.

title: Heavy Periods (Menorrhagia): Causes, Symptoms & When to See a Doctor
excerpt: Soaking through pads every hour or passing large clots? Learn what causes heavy menstrual bleeding, from uterine fibroids to hormone imbalances, and effective treatments.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
What Constitutes Abnormally Heavy Menstrual Bleeding?

Menorrhagia is the clinical term for menstrual periods with abnormally heavy or prolonged bleeding. While individual flow varies, clinical menorrhagia is defined as menstrual loss exceeding 80 mL per cycle, or bleeding that lasts longer than 7 consecutive days.

Common Indicators You May Have Menorrhagia

  • Soaking through one or more sanitary pads or tampons every hour for several consecutive hours
  • Needing to wake up at night to change menstrual protection
  • Passing blood clots larger than a 1-rupee coin
  • Restricting daily social or work activities due to fear of leaking
  • Experiencing chronic fatigue, breathlessness, or being diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia

Underlying Clinical Causes

  • Hormonal Imbalance (Anovulatory Cycles): Without regular ovulation, progesterone is not produced, causing the endometrium to overgrow and shed heavily. This is common in PCOS and perimenopause.
  • Uterine Fibroids: Benign muscular tumors of the uterine wall that expand endometrial surface area and disrupt normal contraction of blood vessels.
  • Endometrial Polyps: Small benign growths in the uterine lining that bleed intermittently.
  • Adenomyosis: When endometrial glands grow deep into the muscular uterine wall, leading to an enlarged, heavy, and painful uterus.
  • Thyroid Disorders: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism disrupt cycle regularity and bleeding control.

Consult a gynecologist for a pelvic ultrasound scan and complete blood count. Treatment options range from medical therapies (tranexamic acid, hormonal birth control, progesterone IUDs) to targeted minimally invasive procedures.

title: Severe Period Pain & Endometriosis: Recognizing the Hidden Symptoms
excerpt: Debilitating period pain is not 'just in your head'. Understand the difference between primary dysmenorrhea and endometriosis, diagnostic steps, and relief options.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Period Cramps vs Endometriosis Pain

Mild menstrual cramping (dysmenorrhea) caused by uterine prostaglandin release is common. However, severe, incapacitating pelvic pain that leaves you bedridden, missing work or school, and unresponsive to standard over-the-counter painkillers is not normal and should never be dismissed.

What is Endometriosis?

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) implants and grows outside the uterine cavity—most commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, outer uterine surface, and pelvic peritoneum. Like normal uterine lining, this tissue thickens, breaks down, and bleeds with each menstrual cycle. Unable to exit the body, trapped blood causes chronic inflammation, severe pain, and scar tissue (adhesions).

Key Symptoms Beyond Period Cramps

  • Chronic Pelvic Pain: Aches that linger throughout the month, not just during bleeding.
  • Deep Dyspareunia: Pain deep inside the pelvis during or after sexual intercourse.
  • Painful Bowel Movements or Urination: Especially prominent during menstrual periods.
  • Difficulty Conceiving: Endometriosis is identified in up to 30–50% of women experiencing unexplained fertility delays.
  • Associated Fatigue and Nausea: Chronic inflammatory responses place significant metabolic stress on the body.

Diagnostic and Management Paths

Consult a gynecological specialist experienced in pelvic pain. Modern high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can detect endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and deep infiltrating nodules. Management encompasses targeted hormonal therapy, anti-inflammatory pain regimens, lifestyle modifications, and laparoscopic excision when indicated.

title: Brown Discharge Before Your Period: Common Causes & When to Worry
excerpt: Wondering why you have brown spotting before your cycle begins? Learn how old blood oxidizes, the role of progesterone, ovulation spotting, and when to get checked.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Why Does Vaginal Discharge Turn Brown?

Vaginal discharge that appears brown or dark rust-colored is simply older blood that has taken longer to exit the uterine cavity. When blood takes time to leave the uterus, it oxidizes upon exposure to oxygen, transforming from bright red to shades of brown or dark copper.

Benign Reasons for Brown Spotting Before a Period

  • Slow Endometrial Shedding: A day or two before full menstrual flow commences, very light initial spotting often oxidizes into brown smears.
  • Luteal Phase Progesterone Fluctuations: If progesterone levels dip slightly a few days before the corpus luteum fully dissolves, slight early shedding of the endometrium may occur.
  • Ovulation Spotting: Approximately 14 days before your period, the sudden estrogen drop during follicle rupture can cause 24 to 48 hours of light brown or pink spotting.
  • Implantation Bleeding: In sexually active women who may have conceived, very light brown discharge 7 to 10 days post-ovulation may represent early implantation.
  • Hormonal Contraceptive Adjustments: Starting or changing birth control pills, IUDs, or contraceptive injections commonly causes breakthrough brown spotting during the first few months.

When to Seek Medical Consultation

Occasional brown spotting a day before your period is generally harmless. However, seek medical evaluation if brown discharge is accompanied by a foul odor, pelvic pain, burning during urination, or if it occurs consistently after sexual intercourse.

title: Irregular Periods & PCOS in India: What to Actually Know
excerpt: Confused about PCOD vs PCOS? A doctor-reviewed guide to irregular periods in India — real causes, when it
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) — Reviewed on 7 September 2026

Irregular periods are common, and PCOS is only one of several possible reasons for them — not the automatic explanation many women assume it is. If you've been told you "probably have PCOD" after one ultrasound, or you're trying to figure out whether your cycle is actually a problem, here's what's real, what's overused, and what to actually do next.

Is PCOD the same as PCOS?

They're closely related, and in everyday conversation in India, people often use them interchangeably — but they're not identical. PCOD (Polycystic Ovarian Disease) describes ovaries releasing immature or partially mature eggs, which can turn into small cysts; it's common — affecting roughly a third of menstruating women by some estimates — and often improves substantially with diet and lifestyle changes alone. PCOS (Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome) is a more involved hormonal condition, where excess androgens (male hormones present in smaller amounts in all women) interfere with ovulation; it's less common, generally needs medical management rather than lifestyle changes alone, and carries higher long-term risks — including insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk — that are worth taking seriously. If you've been told you have "cysts on your ovaries" from a scan, that alone isn't automatically a PCOS diagnosis — more on that below.

PCOS is common in India

More common than most people expect, but the exact number depends heavily on which diagnostic criteria a study used — that's why you'll see very different figures quoted. Indian studies have found rates ranging from around 3.7% to over 22% depending on the region and criteria applied, with several major studies clustering around 9–18%. What's consistent across the research is that it's genuinely common, not a rare diagnosis, and not something to feel isolated about.

Actual symptoms of PCOS

The most common signs are irregular or absent periods, excess facial or body hair growth, acne, hair thinning on the scalp, and weight gain that's disproportionately around the abdomen. Not every woman with PCOS has every symptom, and the severity varies a lot from person to person — which is part of why it's easy to either miss or over-diagnose without a proper clinical workup.

Is every irregular cycle a sign of PCOS?

No — and this is worth saying plainly, because it's one of the most over-applied assumptions in casual conversation about periods. Thyroid problems, high stress, significant weight change, certain medications, perimenopause, and simply the first couple of years after your first period can all cause irregular cycles without PCOS being involved at all. PCOS is one real and common cause, not the default explanation.

How PCOS is actually diagnosed

Properly, it requires meeting at least two of three criteria (the Rotterdam criteria, the standard most Indian gynaecologists use): irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or blood-test signs of excess androgens, and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound. That last point matters: an ultrasound showing multiple small follicles on its own is not sufficient for a diagnosis — it's genuinely common for a scan alone to be over-interpreted as "PCOS" without the other two criteria being checked. If that's what happened to you, it's entirely reasonable to ask your doctor which criteria were actually used.

Can PCOD or PCOS be cured?

PCOD often improves substantially, sometimes resolves largely, with sustained diet and lifestyle changes. PCOS is generally described as manageable rather than curable — many women get their cycle, symptoms, and long-term health risks well under control with the right combination of lifestyle changes and medication, but it's usually an ongoing management relationship with a doctor rather than a one-time fix.

Does PCOS mean I can't get pregnant?

No — PCOS is a leading cause of ovulation-related fertility difficulty, but it is very much not the same as infertility. Many women with PCOS conceive naturally, sometimes with a longer timeline or with support like ovulation-inducing medication. If you have PCOS and are trying to conceive, that's a conversation worth having early with your gynaecologist rather than waiting, since there's a lot that can help.

Period tracking with PCOD / PCOS

Keep logging even when the pattern looks messy — the value shifts from "predicting my next period" to "showing my doctor what's actually been happening" over the last three to six months. Don't expect a next-period prediction to be reliable with a genuinely irregular cycle; that's not the tracker failing, it's an accurate reflection of an unpredictable cycle. What's genuinely useful is the symptom log: hair, skin, weight, and cycle-length patterns over time are exactly what a gynaecologist needs to see.

Lifestyle changes for PCOS

For PCOD and milder PCOS presentations, the most consistently evidence-backed changes are regular physical activity, a diet that manages blood sugar and weight (particularly reducing refined carbohydrates and sugar), consistent sleep, and stress management — all of which influence the hormonal signals involved. These help many women meaningfully, but they're not a guaranteed fix for everyone, especially with more pronounced PCOS, and they don't replace medical management when it's needed.

When should I actually see a gynaecologist about irregular periods?

If your cycles have been consistently irregular for several months, you've gone three months or more without a period (and aren't pregnant or breastfeeding), you're noticing new hair growth, acne, or hair thinning alongside irregular cycles, or you're trying to conceive and it isn't happening — all of these are reasonable, non-alarmist reasons to book an appointment rather than wait it out.

Frequently asked questions

Is PCOD dangerous?
Generally less concerning than PCOS and often responds well to lifestyle changes, but it's still worth a doctor's confirmation rather than self-diagnosing from symptoms alone.
Will losing weight cure my PCOS?
It can meaningfully improve symptoms and cycle regularity for many women, especially with PCOD or milder PCOS, but it isn't a guaranteed cure for everyone and shouldn't replace medical follow-up.
Can I use MiGynae's period tracker even with irregular cycles?
Yes — it's actually one of the most useful things you can do, since a logged pattern over months is exactly what helps your doctor understand what's happening. Just don't expect precise "next period" predictions with a very irregular cycle.

Log your pattern, not just your memory

Whether your cycle is irregular or you're managing PCOS, MiGynae's free tracker helps you build the exact pattern your gynaecologist needs to see — symptoms, cycle length, and flow, all in one place, all free.
