content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) — Reviewed on 4 September 2026

MiGynae's period tracker gives you freedom to track your periods and also predict when they are coming next. No subscription to unlock your own cycle history, no ads between you and your data. Log a few periods and it starts predicting your next one, your likely fertile window, and the patterns worth mentioning to your doctor. Here's exactly how it works, how accurate it really is, and what to do when it gets something wrong — because it will, sometimes, and that's worth understanding rather than panicking about.
"Ready to start tracking your periods? Try Free Period Tracker in MiGynae App — it's amazing."
▶ Download MiGynae — Android  Download MiGynae — iPhone

This is how a period tracker actually works

At its simplest, you tell it when your period starts. Do that for two or three cycles and the app has enough to calculate your average cycle length — the gap between day one of one period and day one of the next — and use it to estimate your next date and your likely ovulation window. Log symptoms, flow, or mood alongside it and the picture gets richer: not just "when," but what tends to happen around that time for you specifically.

The important part is that word "average." A tracker isn't reading your body in real time; it's pattern-matching against your own history. That's why it gets more useful the longer you use it, and a little rough around the edges in the first month or two, or right after something in your cycle changes.

A "normal" menstrual cycle

Cycle length is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. The number most people have heard is 28 days, but that's a textbook average, not a rule — most doctors consider anywhere from 21 to 35 days normal for adults, and a wider range, sometimes up to 45 days, is expected for teenagers whose cycles are still settling into a rhythm. It's also normal for the length to shift a little from month to month even in someone with no underlying issue at all — a cycle isn't a metronome.

Are period tracker apps actually accurate?

As accurate as the data you feed it, and only as predictable as your own biology allows. If your cycles run fairly consistently, predictions tend to land within a day or two. If they vary more — which is common, more common than the "perfect 28-day cycle" idea would suggest — predictions will be rougher, and that's not the app malfunctioning, it's the app honestly reflecting a body that doesn't run on a fixed schedule. Treat every prediction as a well-informed estimate, not a guarantee, especially in your first few months of tracking.

Why did my tracker predict the wrong date this month?

A handful of things routinely throw predictions off, and none of them mean the app is broken: stress, travel and jet lag, illness or fever, a noticeable change in weight, poor sleep, or simply forgetting to log a cycle. One missed prediction is normal. What's actually useful is watching whether it becomes a pattern — that's a conversation worth having with your doctor, not with the app.

Can stress, travel, or illness really delay my period?

Yes, genuinely. The part of your brain that regulates your reproductive hormones — the hypothalamus — is sensitive to physical and emotional stress signals. Significant stress, a long-haul flight, or being unwell can delay ovulation, which pushes your period later than expected as a downstream effect. It's a real physiological response, not "just in your head."

Can a period tracker help me get pregnant, or help me avoid pregnancy?

It can give you a reasonable estimate of your fertile window if you're trying to conceive, based on your logged history — a useful starting point, not a precision instrument. What it should not be used for is contraception on its own. Ovulation can shift for all the reasons above, and relying on a predicted "safe" window to avoid pregnancy carries real risk, especially with an irregular cycle. If fertility planning — in either direction — is your main goal, a dedicated ovulation-tracking approach with more inputs (basal body temperature, cervical mucus, ovulation strips) gives you a much clearer picture; we cover that in a companion article on MiGynae's free ovulation tracker.

Track these besides just your period dates

Flow (light, medium, heavy), cramps or pain, mood, spotting, sleep, and any unusual discharge are all worth a tap. None of it takes more than a few seconds to log, but months of it adds up to something genuinely useful: a real pattern you can show your doctor instead of trying to remember, mid-appointment, whether last month's cramps were actually worse than usual.

When to do a pregnancy test if your period is late

As general guidance: if you're sexually active and your period is more than about a week late, taking a pregnancy test is a reasonable next step. If your cycle is absent or wildly irregular for three months or more, that's worth a doctor's visit rather than more waiting. This is deliberately general — anything that's persistent or worrying you is always worth an actual conversation with your gynaecologist rather than more Googling.

Period tracker or ovulation tracker

A period tracker logs your periods and estimates your next one and your general fertile window from that history. An ovulation tracker zooms in much further on that fertile window specifically, using more detailed signals to narrow down your most fertile days. If you're just trying to understand your own cycle, the period tracker alone does the job. If you're actively trying to conceive — or trying not to — the ovulation tracker is the more precise tool; see our companion guide on MiGynae's free ovulation tracker.

Tracking periods after pregnancy, breastfeeding, or stopping birth control

Yes, and it's normal for it to look messy for a while. Postpartum cycles can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months to return, especially with exclusive breastfeeding, which naturally suppresses ovulation. Coming off hormonal birth control can also mean a few irregular cycles while your body re-establishes its own rhythm. Keep logging through it — the app just needs a little more time and data to catch up, the same way it would for anyone starting fresh.

When should my daughter start tracking her period?

Right from her first period is fine. It's normal for cycles to be irregular for the first couple of years after that as the body matures, so don't expect clean, predictable patterns immediately — the value early on is simply learning her own rhythm and having something concrete to mention to a doctor if anything feels off, rather than relying on memory alone.

title: Does the Safe Period Method Actually Prevent Pregnancy?
excerpt: A gynaecologist-reviewed, straight answer on whether the
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) — Reviewed on 19 September 2026

Short answer — no, it does not. The "safe period" — avoiding sex around your calculated fertile window — is a real method with a real name (the rhythm method, or calendar method), and it is not a reliable method for avoiding pregnancy. It's considered only about 75% effective, with a roughly 25% failure rate, meaning something like 1 in 4 women using it as their only method will get pregnant within a year — and that's a really high risk.
"Get a clearer picture of your cycle with MiGynae's Free Ovulation Tracker."
▶ Download MiGynae — Android  Download MiGynae — iPhone

What is the "safe period" or rhythm method, exactly?

It's the practice of avoiding unprotected sex during your estimated fertile window. During the days when ovulation is not likely, couples have unprotected intercourse. It's one form of what's more broadly called "fertility awareness" or "natural family planning."

How do you find your unsafe days?

Every month, your body releases one egg. If the egg meets a sperm, a baby can start to form. The "safe period" method tries to find the days when this can happen, so you can avoid sex on those days.

But we cannot see the exact day the egg comes out. Sperm can also survive inside your body for up to 5 days, and the egg lives for only about 1 day. So the unsafe days are not one day — they are a group of days. This method helps you find that group with a simple calculation.

How is the "safe period" usually calculated?

The traditional calendar method works off your shortest and longest cycles over at least six months. The logic rests on sperm surviving up to five days inside the body and an egg being viable for roughly 24 hours after ovulation.

How effective is it, really?

With typical, real-world use, it's considered about 75% effective — a roughly 25% failure rate over a year of use as a sole method. That's dramatically less reliable than condoms, hormonal methods, or IUDs. The gap between how effective people assume it is and how effective it actually is, is exactly where unplanned pregnancies happen.

Why is it so much less reliable than other methods?

Because it depends entirely on a prediction, and ovulation is genuinely not that predictable. Stress, illness, travel, and normal month-to-month variation can all shift when you actually ovulate — sometimes earlier, sometimes later than your calculated window. The method assumes every cycle will be consistent, but that's not the case for many women, who have irregular, unpredictable cycles.

Can a period tracker app calculate my "safe days" for me?

A period tracker lets you know about ovulation, so it's tempting to assume that if it can tell you your fertile period, the remaining days must be a safe period. An ovulation tracker is good for estimating your fertile window, but it's not reliable for calculating a genuinely "safe" period. If an app's "safe days" feature is being used as your only method of avoiding pregnancy, it's worth understanding that clearly before relying on it.

Does having an irregular cycle make this method riskier?

Significantly, yes. The entire calculation depends on a consistent, trackable pattern. With an irregular cycle, predicting ovulation becomes far less accurate, which makes the "safe" window considerably less safe. If your cycles vary a lot month to month, this method carries meaningfully more risk for you.

Is the rhythm method the same as the "withdrawal method"?

No — they're often mentioned in the same breath but are different methods. The rhythm method is about timing (avoiding sex during the fertile window); withdrawal is about a physical act during sex (withdrawing before ejaculation) regardless of timing. Some people combine both, but each carries its own separate, and similarly imperfect, failure rate.

What are more reliable alternatives if I want to avoid pregnancy?

Condoms, oral contraceptive pills, IUDs (copper or hormonal), and implants all have meaningfully lower failure rates than the calendar method, with IUDs and implants being the most effective, "set and forget" options. The right choice depends on your health history, whether you're breastfeeding, your future family planning timeline, and personal preference — genuinely worth a direct conversation with your gynaecologist rather than choosing based on what a friend uses.

Does tracking still have a place if I know it's not fully reliable?

Yes — tracking your cycle is still genuinely useful for understanding your body, planning around your period, and noticing patterns worth flagging to a doctor. The issue isn't tracking itself, it's leaning on it alone as your only method to prevent pregnancy. Many people combine cycle tracking with a backup method during the fertile window specifically, which meaningfully improves overall effectiveness.

Frequently asked questions

Is the safe period 100% effective if my cycle is very regular?
No method except abstinence from sex is 100% effective. A very regular cycle improves the accuracy of the calculation, but stress, illness, and normal biological variation can still shift ovulation unexpectedly.
Can I combine the safe period method with a tracker app for better protection?
Using a tracker plus a backup method (like condoms) during your fertile window is more effective than the calendar method alone, but it's still not as reliable as a dedicated contraceptive method — talk to your doctor about what fits your situation.
Does this method protect against STIs?
No — it offers no protection against sexually transmitted infections. Only barrier methods like condoms do.

Medically reviewed by Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) — Reviewed on 19 September 2026

MiGynae's kick tracker is free and helps you log your baby's movements from the point they become countable, so you build a clear sense of your own baby's normal pattern — something worth knowing well before you'd ever need to notice a change in it. Here's when to start, how to count properly, and what's genuinely normal.
"Get to know your baby's pattern — try the Free Kick Tracker in the MiGynae App."

When do babies start kicking, and when should I start counting kicks?

Most women first feel movement somewhere between 18 and 24 weeks — earlier if it's not your first pregnancy, since you already know what to look for. Feeling movement is different from formal kick counting, though: most doctors suggest starting deliberate, daily kick counts from around 28 weeks, once movement is frequent and established enough to track a reliable pattern.

How many kicks should I feel, and how often is that normal?

There are two well-established but slightly different clinical approaches here, and it's worth knowing both rather than picking one blindly. One common benchmark: feeling 10 movements — kicks, flutters, rolls, anything — within about 2 hours is considered reassuring. The other approach, used by the NHS in the UK, deliberately avoids a fixed number altogether: the guidance there is that there's no universal "normal count," and what matters far more is learning your own baby's usual pattern and noticing any real change from it, at any time of day.

Which one should you use?
Both are legitimate — ask your own doctor which approach they'd like you to follow, and use MiGynae's tracker to log against whichever method they recommend. What matters most isn't the exact number, it's building a clear sense of your baby's normal pattern early, so a real change is obvious later.

How do I actually count kicks — a step-by-step method?

A simple, widely used method: pick a time your baby is normally active (often after a meal), sit or lie on your left side to help blood flow, and time how long it takes to feel 10 movements — count kicks, flutters, rolls, and swishes, not just hard kicks. Do this around the same time each day so you're comparing like with like.

What counts as a "kick"? Do flutters, hiccups, and rolls count too?

Yes — count anything you can distinctly feel: kicks, flutters, rolls, stretches, and swishes. Rhythmic, repetitive twitching is often hiccups rather than a kick; it's fine to note it, but it's a different sensation and some trackers separate it out, since hiccups don't reflect the same kind of active movement.

Why does my baby kick more at night or after I eat?

Babies have their own sleep-wake cycles in the womb, and many are more active in the evening. A rise in your blood sugar after eating, and simply sitting still enough to notice movement you'd otherwise miss while busy during the day, both contribute to that "more active at night" feeling too.

How can I get my baby to move if I'm trying to do a count?

Having a cold drink, eating something sweet, and lying down on your left side in a quiet spot are the most commonly suggested ways to encourage movement for a count — babies often respond within 10–20 minutes. If nothing happens after trying this, that's exactly the situation covered in our companion guide on reduced movement.

Do kicks get weaker or less frequent near the due date because there's less room?

This is a common but incorrect assumption. Movement should not meaningfully decrease as you approach your due date — if anything, a real, noticeable drop late in pregnancy is one of the more important signals to act on, not dismiss as "running out of room." We cover exactly what to do about that in the companion article below.

Is it normal for kicks to hurt or feel like they're in my ribs?

Yes, this is common, especially in the third trimester as your baby grows and has less room to move — sharp jabs under the ribs are a frequent complaint and not usually a concern on their own. Shifting position or gently pressing back where you feel it often helps.

How accurate is a kick counter app — can it replace a doctor visit or NST?

A kick counter is an awareness and pattern-tracking tool, not a diagnostic device — it can't replace a non-stress test (NST) or a doctor's evaluation. Its real value is helping you notice, early and clearly, when something is different from your baby's usual pattern, so you know when it's time to get that professional evaluation rather than waiting and wondering.

Is kick counting necessary for every pregnancy, or only high-risk ones?

It's specifically recommended for higher-risk pregnancies, but it's genuinely useful for any pregnancy — it costs nothing, takes a few minutes a day, and builds exactly the kind of awareness that helps you act quickly if something does change.

How do I record kick counts so I can show my doctor a pattern?

Start logging the date and time in the kick tracker, roughly what time you counted, and how long it took to reach your target count. A few weeks of this turns "I think movement has been normal" into an actual pattern you can describe precisely — genuinely useful at a checkup, and essential if you ever need to explain a change.

I have an anterior placenta and can't feel kicks clearly — what should I do?

An anterior placenta (at the front of the uterus) can cushion and muffle movement, so it's common to feel kicks later and less distinctly. Keep tracking anyway using whatever you can feel as your own baseline — your "normal" will just look a little different, and that's fine as long as you know your own pattern.

Twin pregnancy — how do I count kicks for two babies?

It's genuinely harder to attribute movement to a specific twin, and most doctors don't expect you to separate them precisely. The practical approach is to track total movement and overall activity level rather than trying to count each baby individually — and to mention the twin pregnancy specifically if you ever need to discuss reduced movement with your doctor, since the guidance can differ slightly.

Frequently asked questions

My baby isn't moving as much today — should I worry?
This deserves a clear, direct answer with real thresholds for when to act — we cover it fully, including exactly when to call your doctor, in a dedicated companion article on reduced fetal movement.
Should I use a home fetal doppler instead of counting kicks?
We cover this specifically in our companion article on reduced movement, since it involves a genuine safety caveat worth reading in full.
Is it ever too early to start using the kick tracker?
You can log movement as soon as you feel it, but formal daily counting is most meaningful from around 28 weeks, once movement is well established.

title: Reduced Fetal Movement: When to Worry, When to Act
excerpt: Baby not kicking as much? A doctor-reviewed, direct guide to what
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Medically reviewed by Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) — Reviewed on 19 September 2026

If your baby is moving noticeably less than their usual pattern, the direct answer is: contact your doctor or maternity unit the same day, not tomorrow morning — reduced movement is one of the few pregnancy symptoms where waiting genuinely isn't the safer choice. Most of the time it turns out to be nothing serious. But it always needs to be checked, every time, without exception.
"Want to explore our Free Kick Counter? Explore the MiGynae app."
▶ Download MiGynae — Android  Download MiGynae — iPhone

My baby isn't moving as much today — should I worry?

Take it seriously enough to act, without assuming the worst. Try the standard approach first: have a cold drink or something to eat, lie down on your left side in a quiet room, and count movements for up to two hours. If you feel fewer than 10 movements in that time, or the pattern feels clearly different from your baby's normal — even if you can't put a number on it — contact your doctor or maternity unit the same day.

When should I go to the hospital or call my doctor for reduced movement?

⚠ Call the same day — visit the hospital right away, if:
  • You count fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours (during your usual active time) after trying to encourage movement
  • You notice any clear reduction or change from your baby's normal pattern (regardless of the exact count)
  • You're generally worried, even without a specific number to point to

Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment, and do not wait until morning if this happens at night — maternity units expect and want these calls at any hour.

Does reduced fetal movement always mean something is wrong?

No — most of the time, a single episode of reduced movement turns out to be reassuring once checked: babies do have quieter periods, and things like your position, blood sugar, or simply being distracted can all affect what you notice. But "usually fine" is exactly why it needs checking every time rather than assumed — the only way to tell a benign quiet spell from something that needs attention is a proper evaluation, not guessing at home.

Should I use a home fetal doppler instead of counting kicks?

This is worth being direct about: relying on a home doppler to reassure yourself instead of getting checked is a real risk, not a safe alternative. A doppler can pick up a heartbeat even when there's an underlying problem, which can give false reassurance and delay getting proper care. If you're worried about movement, the right step is contacting your doctor or maternity unit, not reaching for a doppler at home.

Can a kick counter app replace a doctor visit or a non-stress test (NST)?

No — a tracker is an awareness tool that helps you notice a change quickly. It cannot assess your baby's wellbeing the way a clinical evaluation or NST can. An NST tells you about the pattern of the heartbeat, and it's very accurate. Its job is to get you to make the call sooner, with a clearer description of what changed, not to replace the call itself.

Is it normal to feel less movement at night versus during the day?

Some variation across the day is normal — many babies do have quieter and more active stretches. The distinction that matters is between your baby's own usual pattern (which can genuinely include a quieter stretch at a particular time) and a real change from that pattern. If you're unsure which one you're seeing, that uncertainty itself is a reasonable enough reason to do a proper count and call if it doesn't reassure you.

What if I've noticed reduced movement more than once this week?

Mention that explicitly when you call — a repeated pattern of reduced movement, even if each individual episode seemed to resolve, is worth flagging clearly rather than treating each occurrence as a separate, isolated event. Doctors want that fuller picture, not just the most recent episode.

Why does this matter more in India specifically?

Routine antenatal monitoring like non-stress tests and regular ultrasounds is less consistently accessible outside major cities in India, which makes learning your own baby's movement pattern — and knowing exactly when to act on a change — a genuinely higher-value safety habit here than in a setting with easy, frequent clinical monitoring. Fetal-movement awareness gaps in Indian antenatal care are a real, documented public health issue, not an abstract concern — this is exactly the kind of practical knowledge a free, accessible tool can help close.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to just wait until my next appointment?
No — reduced movement should be checked the same day it's noticed, not held for a scheduled appointment days or weeks away.
Will I be told I'm overreacting if it turns out to be nothing?
No — maternity units and doctors genuinely expect and welcome these calls. Being checked and reassured is exactly how the system is meant to work, not a bother.
Does an anterior placenta or being a first-time mother change this advice?
It can affect how early and clearly you feel movement in general, but it doesn't change the advice here — any noticeable change from your own normal pattern, whatever that baseline looks like for you, is still worth calling about the same day.

medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
If you want a smoother, more confident normal delivery — start preparing BEFORE labour begins.
1

Antenatal Foundation (0–20 Weeks)

First rule: If you are a LOW-RISK pregnancy — stay ACTIVE.

✓ Confirm with your doctor
  • No cervical shortening
  • No cervical dilation
  • No bleeding / complications

💡 What most women do wrong

They become overly cautious → stop movement → body becomes stiff → labour becomes difficult

✅ What you SHOULD do
  • Continue daily routine work
  • Avoid unnecessary bed rest
  • Do not panic with mild pulling pains

🏃‍♀️ 3 Must-Do Exercises (0–20 Weeks)

Walking (20–30 min daily) Improves circulation & stamina
Pelvic Tilts (5–10 reps, 2–3 times/day) Strengthens pelvic muscles
Deep Breathing Practice (5 min daily) Starts training your body for labour
🎯 Goal: Build a flexible + strong body early
2

Smart Activity Plan (20–36 Weeks)

Now your preparation becomes targeted for labour. Progress gradually every 4 weeks:

📍 20–24 Weeks
  • Walking daily (30 min)
  • Butterfly pose (gentle)
Focus: Flexibility begins
📍 24–28 Weeks
  • Walking continues
  • Butterfly pose
  • Start Pelvic Opening Movements (Duck walk – mild, assisted)
Focus: Hip opening
📍 28–32 Weeks
  • Walking
  • Butterfly pose
  • Add Squats (supported, 5–10 reps)
  • Cat-Cow Stretch (very important)
Focus: Pelvis mobility + baby positioning
📍 32–34 Weeks — Start Active Labour Preparation
  • Walking (30–40 min daily)
  • Supported squats (8–10 reps)
  • Cat-Cow stretch
  • Pelvic rocking
  • Birthing ball sitting & gentle bouncing
Focus: Improve flexibility + begin baby descent preparation
📍 34–36 Weeks — Intensify Your Preparation
  • Walking (essential daily)
  • Squats (increase frequency)
  • Birthing ball (15–20 mins/day)
  • Pelvic rocking (regular)
  • Lunges (supported) → improves pelvic opening
  • Side-lying leg lifts → strengthens pelvic muscles
Focus: Open pelvis + improve baby positioning
📍 36+ Weeks — Final Labour Readiness Phase

Now your body needs maximum support for labour. Make movement your routine throughout the day.

🔥 Must-Do Exercises

Deep Squats / Malasana (supported) Opens pelvic outlet
Birthing Ball Exercises Sitting, bouncing, circular hip movements
Pelvic Rocking (frequent) Helps baby descend
Walking (multiple short rounds daily) Encourages natural labour onset
Cat-Cow Stretch Improves baby alignment
Butterfly Pose Keeps pelvic muscles relaxed
Stair Climbing (if comfortable) Helps engagement of baby

📅 Daily Routine

Morning
Walk + Squats
Afternoon
Birthing ball + Pelvic rocking
Evening
Walk + Butterfly pose
Night
Deep breathing + Relaxation
🎯 Focus: Encourage baby descent + natural labour onset
Always stop if:
  • Pain increases
  • Giddiness
  • Bleeding / leaking
✓ Important reminders
  • Stay active — but don't exhaust yourself
  • Take breaks
  • Stay hydrated
  • Consistency matters more than intensity
3

Diet for Easier Labour (32+ Weeks)

This is where most people ignore preparation. From 32–34 weeks onwards, shift to a labour-supportive diet.

✅ What Helps
  • Protein-rich foods (dal, paneer, sprouts) — builds stamina for labour
  • Iron + hydration — prevents exhaustion
  • Dates (2–3 daily) — natural energy
  • Coconut water — electrolytes
  • Banana — quick energy
  • Fibre-rich diet — prevents constipation for a smoother labour experience
✗ Avoid
  • Heavy oily food
  • Excess sugar
  • Overeating at night
🎯 Goal: Light body + high energy = better pushing ability
4

What to Discuss with Your Doctor

A prepared mother has a smoother journey. Ask THESE important questions:

"Am I a candidate for normal delivery?"
"What is my cervical status?" (length + dilation)
"Can we wait for spontaneous labour if safe?"
"If leaking happens, can induction be tried first?"
"When is C-section truly required?"
🎯 Realistic Expectations
  • Cervix needs to soften + open gradually
  • Labour can take hours — not minutes
  • Pain is progressive and purposeful

Understanding this reduces fear → improves outcomes

5

Labour Management (Most Important)

Now comes the real game: PATIENCE + TECHNIQUE

🌀 Breathing — Your Biggest Tool
  • Slow deep inhale → controlled exhale
  • Do NOT panic-breathe

This reduces pain perception significantly

🏃 Movement During Labour
  • Walking
  • Birthing ball exercises
  • Changing positions

Helps baby descend faster

🏃‍♀ Positions That Help
  • Squatting
  • Side-lying
  • Leaning forward
Very Important

Do NOT push early. Push ONLY when your doctor advises.

💉 Epidural?

You can ask for an epidural if:

  • Pain is unbearable
  • Labour is prolonged

It is a safe option when used correctly.

  Follow these guidelines only if your doctor has confirmed a low-risk pregnancy with no contraindications. Always consult your healthcare provider before starting any new exercise or diet routine.

title: The Epidural, Explained
excerpt: The epidural explained: what it is, what to expect, myths vs facts, and the right questions to ask your doctor or anaesthetist.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
An epidural can make labour far more comfortable while you stay awake and in control. Knowing how it works takes the fear out of the decision.
1

What an epidural is

A pain-relief injection given in your lower back during labour. It numbs the lower half of your body, so contractions hurt far less, while you stay fully awake and alert. A thin, soft tube is left in place so the medicine can be topped up as your labour goes on.

When can you ask?

When labour pain becomes hard to manage. It is usually given once labour is well established, but the timing is decided with your doctor and anaesthetist based on how you are progressing. There is no prize for suffering — it is okay to ask.

2

What to expect

1
Getting it placedYou will sit or lie curled forward and stay as still as you can for a few minutes.
2
A gentle startA small local injection numbs the skin first, so placing the tube feels like pressure, not sharp pain.
3
Relief beginsThe pain usually eases within about 10 to 20 minutes.
4
You will be monitoredYour blood pressure and your baby's heartbeat are watched closely. You may need a small tube to empty your bladder.
5
Heavy legsYour legs will feel heavy or numb. That is normal and wears off after birth.
3

Myths vs facts

MythIt causes lifelong back pain.
FactResearch does not support this. Some soreness at the spot for a day or two can happen.
MythIt always leads to a C-section.
FactIt does not. It may make pushing a little longer, and sometimes a little help is needed to birth the baby.
MythYou cannot push with an epidural.
FactYou can. Your team guides you on when to push, and many women still feel pressure.
Good to know

Most women do very well. Some feel shivering, itching, or a short drop in blood pressure that the team manages quickly. A bad headache afterwards is uncommon, and serious problems are rare. A few conditions — like certain bleeding problems, some spine issues, or blood-thinning medicines — can make an epidural unsuitable, so your anaesthetist will always check first.

4

Ask your doctor or anaesthetist

A few good questions to feel ready:

  1. Am I a good candidate for an epidural?
  2. When can I have it, and is it ever too late?
  3. Will I still be able to move or push?
  4. What side effects should I watch for?

title: C-Section (Caesarean / LSCS) Guide: What to Expect & Recovery
excerpt: A caesarean (LSCS) guide: the essentials, recovering well, warning signs to watch for, and reassurance that it is still your birth.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
A caesarean is a safe, very common way to bring your baby into the world. Knowing what happens and how to heal helps you recover with confidence.
1

The essentials

What it is

A safe, very common surgery that delivers your baby through a cut in your lower tummy. You are usually awake, with a spinal injection that numbs you from the waist down, so you can meet your baby right away. A tube (catheter) drains your bladder and stays in for a while.

Why it may be chosen

Sometimes planned, sometimes decided in labour — for reasons like a breech baby, a low-lying placenta, the baby not coming down, or signs the baby should be born quickly. It is a decision made for safety, never a failure on your part.

2

Recovering well: the must-knows

  • It is major surgery. Full healing takes about 6 weeks — be patient with yourself.
  • Start gentle movement early — it helps prevent clots and speeds healing.
  • Support your stitches with a hand or pillow when you cough, laugh or get up.
  • Take pain relief as prescribed — you do not need to suffer.
  • Avoid heavy lifting — nothing heavier than your baby at first.
  • Feed in positions that keep the baby's weight off your wound.
When to call your doctor

After a caesarean, get help if you notice:

  • Fever or chills
  • Redness, pus, swelling or a gap in the wound
  • Heavy bleeding, or foul-smelling discharge
  • Severe or increasing tummy pain
  • Pain, redness or swelling in your calf
  • Breathlessness or chest pain
It is still your birth

A caesarean is a real birth, and a brave one. If you feel any sadness that it did not go as planned, that feeling is valid and it passes. Your bond with your baby and your feeding are exactly the same.

title: Postpartum Recovery Guide & Depression Signs
excerpt: Learn postpartum depression signs, safe recovery tips, wound care and breastfeeding guidance after delivery. Expert-reviewed support from MiGynae.
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
No one prepares you for this part… Your body, hormones, sleep, emotions — everything changes after delivery… and the unexpected happens.

This guide will help you:

  • Recover faster
  • Avoid common mistakes
  • Know what is normal vs not
  • Take care of yourself while caring for baby
1

What to Expect Immediately After Delivery

📲 Need daily postpartum guidance?

MiGynae covers pregnancy and post-delivery — all in one place.

Play Store App Store
  • Bleeding (like heavy periods) is normal, but if you are changing pads every hour, that is not normal — seek care.
  • Pain in abdomen / stitches is common; you may ask for a different painkiller or for medication earlier if needed.
  • Weakness and exhaustion are common — keep sipping fluids.
  • Start breastfeeding within 1 hour when possible.
  • Gentle movement in bed is allowed. After a normal delivery you may start a supported walk soon after. After a caesarean, move your legs while lying down as soon as you have leg sensation.
  • Soft diet or liquids are usually fine soon after a normal delivery. After an uncomplicated caesarean, you may start sipping fluids after 4–6 hours (as your team advises).
  • You may feel dizzy the first time you stand — ask someone to support you and stay hydrated.
  • After a caesarean, your doctor may allow you to turn in bed around 8–16 hours and walking between 12–24 hours, depending on your case.
  • A catheter usually stays for at least 24 hours after a caesarean.
2

What to Expect in the First 4–7 Days

  • Your body is healing. The uterus is shrinking — you may feel cramps.
  • Vaginal discharge (lochia) continues; bleeding may be mild to moderate, not heavy. If it is heavy, inform your gynaecologist.
  • Stitches may feel sore after either a normal delivery or caesarean. Cold packs on the area can help healing (as advised).

Understand lochia (bleeding — what is normal?)

  • Discharge (lochia) often changes colour over weeks: red → pink → brown → yellowish.
  • Contact your doctor for very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad hourly), foul-smelling discharge, or large clots.
3

Wound care: episiotomy vs caesarean

Practical tips — always follow your own doctor’s instructions.

Aspect Episiotomy (normal delivery stitch) C-section (abdominal stitch)
Water & cleaning
  • Use warm water after every urination / defecation. Use antiseptic liquid or ointment, especially after passing stool.
  • Gently pat dry (don’t rub). Clean from front to back.
  • Sitz bath (10–15 min, 1–2 times/day) can help — after bleeding has reduced, as advised.
  • You can usually bathe after 24–48 hours (as advised).
  • Let water run gently over the incision; dressing in hospital, then antiseptic care as instructed.
  • Avoid moisture trapped on the wound — change wet dressings early or use waterproof dressing if advised.
Dressing / exposure
  • Often no dressing needed.
  • Keep the area dry and open; avoid very tight clothing.
  • Dressing for a few days depending on incision type.
  • Once healed, keep clean and dry (antiseptic powder or ointment only if prescribed).
Pain relief & comfort
  • Ice packs in the first 24 hours can reduce swelling.
  • Sitz bath can soothe.
  • Soft cushion or donut pillow when sitting.
  • Pain medicines as prescribed.
  • Use pillow support when getting up; avoid sudden twisting.
  • Push more through hands and heels when moving, not through the stitch line.
  • Pain medicines as prescribed.
4

What to avoid

  • Tight underwear
  • Constipation / straining — use stool softeners if prescribed
  • Ignoring increasing pain, swelling, pus, or throbbing pain
  • Lifting baby incorrectly — bend from the knees
  • Tight waistbands over stitches or incision
  • Wet or sweaty incision area
5

Warning signs — seek care

🚨 Get medical help if you notice
  • Increasing pain or swelling
  • Foul smell or abnormal discharge
  • Severe difficulty sitting or walking
  • Redness, pus, or a gap in stitches
  • Fever
6

Postpartum exercises (week-wise)

Start slow, progress smartly, build stamina. Don’t stay in bed.

  • Start walking early, or as your doctor advises.
  • Avoid complete bed rest when safe — it helps prevent clots, improves healing, mood, and digestion.
📍 2–6 weeks: what you should do

If you had a normal delivery

  • Start moving gently.
  • Kegel exercises daily (very important).
  • Walk every day — slowly increase time.
  • Light stretching for back and hips.
  • Simple pelvic movements like butterfly when comfortable.

Your body is ready to regain strength — just don’t overdo it.

If you had a C-section

  • Your body needs a little more protection.
  • Start Kegels (safe and important).
  • Walk in short intervals — avoid long pushes at first.
  • Deep breathing exercises.
  • Keep movements gentle — avoid strain on the abdomen.

Healing is happening inside — respect that pace.

📍 6–10 weeks: moving forward (only after your doctor says you’re ready)

After normal delivery

  • Continue Kegels.
  • Increase walking pace gradually.
  • Light yoga or simple exercises.
  • Begin mild core work and squats when cleared.

After C-section

  • Go slow — your scar is still healing.
  • Increase walking time gradually.
  • Continue Kegels.
  • Very gentle core activation.
  • Light yoga without pressure on stitches — when approved.
For all mothers
  • If something hurts — stop.
  • Don’t compare your recovery with others.
  • Slow progress is still progress.
  • Always discuss changes with your doctor before intensifying activity.
7

Breastfeeding basics

Wondering if your baby is getting enough milk?

Tap here to read the signs — and download the MiGynae app for the full article and tools.

8

Eat to recover (diet after delivery)

  • Include protein (dal, paneer, eggs if non-veg), iron + calcium, and warm fluids.
  • Indian staples like panjiri / gond, ajwain water, and jeera water — in moderation.
  • Warm fluids can support recovery and breastfeeding.
✗ Limit or avoid
  • Excess ghee or oil
  • Junk food and excess sweets
  • Foods that trigger acidity for you
9

Take care of your mental health

  • Mood swings are common; you may feel overwhelmed.
  • Ask for help if you have continuous sadness or anxiety, especially if bonding with baby feels difficult.
  • Postpartum depression is real and treatable — reach out early.
  • You will often be tired. You don’t have to do everything alone — ask for help and sleep when baby sleeps when you can.
  • Family support matters. Delegate tasks; accept help. Focus on your recovery and the baby.
  • Be kind to yourself — your body has done something incredible.
  This guide is for general education only. Every delivery and recovery is different. Always follow your obstetrician or healthcare team’s advice, especially if you had complications, pain, fever, or heavy bleeding.

title: Partner's Guide to Supporting Pregnancy & Labour

content:
You do not have to fix everything. Being present, patient and informed is the support she will remember most.
1

The little things mean everything

  • Listen. Often she needs to be heard, not fixed.
  • Take chores off her plate before she asks.

In the labour room

After the baby comes

  • Bring her water and food, especially while she is feeding.

title: Pregnancy Beauty & Salon Guide
excerpt: Skin care, hair colour, facials and salon treatments in pregnancy: what
medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)
content:
Reviewed and approved by Dr. Shuchita Batra Goyal, MS (OBGY) — Founder, MiGynae App

Your skin absorbs a little of what you put on it. Most beauty routines are fine in pregnancy — only a few ingredients and treatments are better paused until after delivery. Here's exactly what's safe for skin, hair and salon visits, and what to skip for now.
"Pregnancy questions at 2 am? Ask MiGynae — free during beta."
▶ Download MiGynae — Android  Download MiGynae — iPhone

Skin care: read the label

Avoid these
  • Retinol or any "retin-" name (Retinol, Retinyl palmitate, Retinaldehyde, Tretinoin, Adapalene, Tazarotene) — vitamin A tablets cause birth defects, so retinoid creams are avoided too.
  • Hydroquinone (skin-lightening creams) — skin absorbs a lot of it, with no proof it's safe in pregnancy.
  • Strong salicylic acid (peels, strong creams) — it's in the aspirin family. A mild face wash is fine.
  • Oxybenzone (chemical sunscreen filter) — absorbed into the blood and may affect hormones.
Use these instead
  • Mineral sunscreen (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) — helps prevent pregnancy dark patches (melasma).
  • Azelaic acid for pimples and dark spots.
  • Low-strength benzoyl peroxide or glycolic acid for acne.
  • Vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid for glow and hydration.
  • Gentle cleanser and a plain moisturiser.
Stretch marks
No cream can fully prevent them. A good moisturiser keeps skin soft and reduces itching.

Hair: colour, treatments and products

Okay, with care
  • Hair colour — wait until after the first 3 months. Use a well-ventilated room, gloves and a patch test. Highlights are better, as less colour touches the scalp.
  • Pure mehndi (henna) is fine.
  • Regular shampoo, conditioner and hair oil are fine. A regular anti-dandruff shampoo is usually fine; ask your doctor about medicated ones.
Wait until after delivery
  • Keratin, smoothening, Brazilian blowout — heating can release formaldehyde gas.
  • Rebonding, strong straightening, perms — harsh chemicals with little safety data.
  • Minoxidil (hair-fall lotion) — absorbed into the body. Not for pregnancy.
  • "Black mehndi" (contains PPD) — can cause a strong allergic reaction.
Postpartum shedding
Hair often looks thicker in pregnancy. Hair fall 2 to 4 months after delivery is common and usually settles on its own.

Facials and salon treatments

Safe
  • Clean-up or simple facial (no peel, no strong chemicals).
  • Threading and waxing — skin is more sensitive now, so test a small area first.
  • Manicure and pedicure in a well-ventilated place.
  • Gentle face and head massage.
Wait until after delivery
  • Chemical peels (salicylic, TCA, retinoid peels).
  • Laser (hair removal, skin resurfacing) — no safety data in pregnancy.
  • Botox and fillers.
  • Microdermabrasion and derma-roller — sensitive skin can get more dark patches.
  • Face bleach and skin-lightening creams.
  • Sauna, steam room, hot tub — overheating is not good for the baby.

4 things to do at the salon

A few habits that make any salon visit safer during pregnancy:

  1. Tell them you are pregnant.
  2. Choose a well-ventilated salon, away from strong smells.
  3. Ask for a patch test before any new product.
  4. After 20 weeks, don't lie flat on your back for long — ask for a pillow to tilt you to one side.

When to call your doctor

⚠ Get medical help if you notice:
  • Strong itching on palms and soles, especially at night, in the last 3 months
  • A rash with blisters
  • Swelling of face or lips, or trouble breathing after a product — go to hospital right away
  • Sudden swelling of face or hands with a bad headache or blurred vision

faqs.answer: A normal menstrual cycle typically ranges between 21 and 35 days, with bleeding lasting 2 to 7 days. Occasional shifts of 2–3 days due to stress or routine changes are common and normal.

faqs.question: How do I know if my period is abnormally heavy?
faqs.answer: Bleeding is abnormally heavy (menorrhagia) if you soak through one or more sanitary pads every 1 to 2 hours, pass clots larger than a coin, or feel unusually weak, pale, or dizzy during your period.

faqs.question: Can stress cause periods to be late or irregular?
faqs.answer: Yes. Severe emotional or physical stress triggers high levels of cortisol, which disrupts the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and can suppress or delay ovulation, leading to late or missed periods.

faqs.question: When should I see a gynaecologist for irregular periods?
faqs.answer: Consult a doctor if your cycles are consistently under 21 or over 35 days, you have missed periods for 3 consecutive months (and are not pregnant), bleed between periods, or have severe pelvic pain.

faqs.question: What is the difference between occasional irregular periods and PCOS?
faqs.answer: Occasional irregularity is usually temporary and triggered by illness, weight changes, or stress. PCOS is a chronic hormonal and metabolic condition characterized by persistent irregular periods, cystic ovaries, acne, and excess androgen symptoms.

medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MS (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)

faqs.question: Are ultrasound scans safe for me and my baby during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes. Diagnostic pregnancy ultrasounds use high-frequency sound waves rather than ionizing radiation (like X-rays). When performed by trained medical professionals for clinical purposes, ultrasound has an exceptional safety record.

faqs.question: Why do I need a full bladder for early pregnancy scans?

The main scans in pregnancy

For early scans, you may be asked to come with a full bladder - drink water and do not pass urine just before.

Wear loose, comfortable clothing for easy belly access.

A cool gel is put on your tummy - it may feel cold, nothing more.

faqs.answer: A combination of 30 minutes of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, or dancing) 4–5 days a week, plus 2 days of strength training or yoga to improve peripheral insulin sensitivity and metabolic rate.

faqs.question: Can diet and exercise cure PCOS permanently?
faqs.answer: PCOS is a chronic metabolic condition that cannot be cured with a one-time pill, but clinical studies prove that adopting consistent dietary and movement habits can fully manage symptoms, restore ovulatory cycles, and prevent long-term complications.

faqs.question: How does sleep and stress management help in PCOS?
faqs.answer: Chronic stress elevates cortisol and worsens insulin resistance, which directly drives up androgen (male hormone) levels. Getting 7 to 8 hours of deep sleep and practicing mindfulness keeps stress hormones in check.

title: PCOD vs PCOS: What's the Difference?

metaDescription: PCOD and PCOS are not the same. Learn the difference, common PCOS symptoms like irregular periods and acne, and when to get checked by a gynaecologist.

medicalReviewer: Dr. Shuchita Batra, MBBS, MS (Obstetrics & Gynaecology)

faqs.question: What is the primary difference between PCOD and PCOS?
faqs.answer: PCOD (Polycystic Ovarian Disease) is an anatomical condition where ovaries release partially mature eggs that turn into cysts, primarily manageable with lifestyle. PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) is a broader metabolic and endocrine disorder involving significant hormonal imbalance, elevated androgens, and systemic metabolic risks.

faqs.question: Is PCOD more common than PCOS?
faqs.answer: Yes. PCOD is very common among young women, often mild, and frequently detected incidentally on an ultrasound. PCOS is less common but more severe, requiring closer medical and endocrine supervision.

faqs.question: Can women with PCOD or PCOS get pregnant naturally?
faqs.answer: Yes. With proper cycle tracking, balanced nutrition, weight management, and medical assistance to induce ovulation if needed, the majority of women with PCOD and PCOS conceive and enjoy healthy pregnancies.

faqs.question: What diagnostic tests are used to detect PCOS?
faqs.answer: A doctor typically assesses your clinical history, performs a pelvic ultrasound to examine ovarian morphology, and orders blood tests for fasting glucose/insulin, LH, FSH, thyroid profile (TSH), prolactin, and free testosterone.

faqs.question: Why does PCOS cause acne and facial hair?
faqs.answer: Elevated insulin levels in PCOS stimulate the ovaries and adrenal glands to produce excess male hormones (androgens like testosterone), which overstimulate oil glands causing stubborn acne and cause hirsutism (coarse hair on chin, upper lip, or abdomen).

Irregular, late or missing periods

faqs.question: What are the most urgent danger signs in a newborn infant?
faqs.answer: Fast breathing (>60 breaths/min), chest indrawing, grunting, blue lips or tongue, refusal to feed, convulsions or fits, fever (>100.4°F/38°C) or cold body (<97.7°F/36.5°C), deep yellow palms/soles, and extreme floppiness. Any single sign requires immediate emergency hospital care.

faqs.question: What should I do if my baby stops breathing or turns bluish?
faqs.answer: Immediately hold the infant upright against your chest, gently clear any obstruction from the mouth/nose, stimulate the baby by rubbing their back or feet, and rush directly to the nearest emergency paediatric hospital.

faqs.question: When is jaundice in a newborn considered an emergency?
faqs.answer: While mild jaundice on day 3–5 is common, jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of birth, or spreading to the abdomen, palms, and soles of the feet with dark urine and pale stools, is dangerous and requires urgent phototherapy evaluation.

faqs.question: Why is a low body temperature dangerous for a newborn?
faqs.answer: Hypothermia in newborns causes rapid energy depletion, low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), and breathing distress. If baby feels cold to touch, initiate skin-to-skin kangaroo care immediately while heading to a doctor.

faqs.question: What are the signs of an infected umbilical cord stump?
faqs.answer: Redness or swelling spreading to the surrounding abdominal skin, foul-smelling pus oozing from the base, or continuous bleeding. This condition (omphalitis) requires urgent paediatric antibiotics.

Newborns can become unwell quickly. Knowing these signs, and acting fast, can save your baby's life. Trust your instinct.

Go to a doctor now if your baby has

Any one of these needs urgent medical care:

  • Trouble breathing fast or noisy breathing, chest pulling in, grunting, or blue lips or tongue
  • Will not feed, or feeds very poorly
  • Very sleepy, floppy, or hard to wake
  • Fits or convulsions
  • Fever, or body cold to the touch
  • Deep yellow skin, or yellow palms and soles
  • Red, swollen, foul-smelling or pus-draining belly button
  • Constant vomiting, a swollen hard tummy, or no urine or stool
  • A weak, high-pitched, or non-stop cry

See exactly what to watch for

Danger signs are easier to recognise when you have seen them. The MiGynae App has short videos on each newborn danger sign - what it looks like and how to handle it - for much better clarity. If you want to be sure, watch them in the app.

What to do right away

Do not wait and watch. Take the baby to your doctor or nearest hospital at once.

Keep the baby warm on the way, skin-to-skin against your chest.

Carry any hospital papers, and call ahead if you can.

Do not give any home remedy or medicine your doctor has not advised.

Until you reach the doctor

  • Hard breathing or blue lips: hold the baby upright against your chest, gently clear the nose, and rush.
  • Fitting or convulsing: lay the baby on their side, put nothing in the mouth, and note how long it lasts.
  • Cold to touch: warm slowly with skin-to-skin and a cap, and cover you both.
  • Feverish: do not wrap tightly, keep the baby cool and comfortable.
  • Awake and able to suck: keep offering breastmilk. Never force-feed a baby who is fitting or very drowsy.

When in doubt, get it checked

You know your baby best. It is always better to see a doctor and be reassured than to wait. With a newborn, never feel shy about asking for help.

faqs.question: Why is feeding colostrum in the first hour essential?
faqs.answer: Colostrum is the thick, nutrient-dense first milk packed with maternal antibodies (IgA), proteins, and gut-protective factors that coat the baby's digestive tract, act as a natural laxative to clear meconium, and provide early immune defense.

faqs.question: How can I tell if my baby has a good breastfeeding latch?
faqs.answer: The baby's mouth should be wide open taking in the nipple and a generous amount of the lower areola. The chin touches the breast, lips are flared outward (not curled inward), and feeding does not cause sharp pinching pain after the initial latch.

faqs.question: How often should a newborn feed?
faqs.answer: Newborns should be fed on demand whenever showing early hunger cues (rooting, lip smacking, hands to mouth), typically 8 to 12 times in 24 hours (every 2 to 3 hours), including during the night.

faqs.question: What are reliable signs that baby is getting enough milk?
faqs.answer: At least 6 heavy wet diapers per day after day 4, 3–4 soft yellow bowel movements, visible/audible swallowing during nursing, content behavior after feeds, and consistent weight gain verified by your paediatrician.

faqs.question: What should I do for sore or cracked nipples?
faqs.answer: Ensure the latch is deep rather than shallow on the nipple tip. Express a few drops of colostrum or breast milk and rub gently onto the nipple to air-dry. If pain persists, consult an IBCLC lactation consultant or gynaecologist.

Start right

Try to feed within the first hour after birth.

The first thick yellow milk (colostrum) is gold - small in amount, full of protection. Do not throw it away.

Keep baby skin-to-skin - it calms baby and helps milk flow.

A good latch

Baby's mouth should be wide open, taking in the nipple and much of the areola - not just the tip.

Chin touches the breast, lips flared out.

A good latch should not hurt - if it pinches, gently break the seal and try again.

How often

Feed on demand, usually every 2 to 3 hours, day and night.

Let baby finish one breast before offering the other.

For the first 6 months, breastmilk is all baby needs - no water or top feed unless your doctor advises.

Feeding is far easier once you have seen it. The MiGynae App has short videos - how to hold your baby and breastfeeding positions - so you can get comfortable and latch right. Watch them in the app.

Drink water each time you feed, and eat well.

Rest when you can - tiredness affects milk.

Sore or cracked nipples and hard, full breasts are common early on and can be managed - do not suffer in silence.

faqs.question: How should I hold and support my newborn baby?
faqs.answer: Always support the baby's head and neck with your hand or arm whenever lifting, holding, or carrying. Newborn neck muscles are weak and cannot support the heavy head on their own for several months.

faqs.question: What are safe sleep guidelines for a newborn?
faqs.answer: Always lay your baby flat on their back on a firm mattress in a separate crib or bassinet in your room. Avoid pillows, quilts, soft toys, loose blankets, and sleeping together on a couch or armchair to prevent suffocation and SIDS.

faqs.question: How do I care for the umbilical cord stump at home?
faqs.answer: Keep the stump clean and dry at all times. Fold the top of the diaper down below the cord to expose it to air. Do not apply oil, turmeric, powders, or antiseptics unless specifically instructed by your paediatrician.

faqs.question: How many layers of clothes should a newborn wear?
faqs.answer: Dress your baby in one more layer of clothing than you are comfortably wearing for the room temperature. Feel their chest or upper back to gauge warmth; hands and feet naturally feel cooler due to developing circulation.

faqs.question: How often should a newborn baby be bathed?
faqs.answer: Give gentle sponge baths until the umbilical cord stump has naturally fallen off and healed. Thereafter, a gentle warm water bath 2 to 3 times a week is sufficient, as daily soaping can dry out sensitive newborn skin.

6 or more wet nappies a day is a good sign of enough milk.

Always lay the baby on the back to sleep, never the tummy.

Use a firm flat surface, with no pillows, soft toys or loose bedding.

Keep the baby's cot in your room for the first few months.

Never sleep with the baby on a sofa or under heavy blankets.

Dress the baby in one more layer than you are wearing, not more.

Check warmth by feeling the chest or back, not the hands or feet.

Keep the umbilical stump clean and dry, and let it fall off on its own.

Fold the nappy below the stump, and put nothing on it unless advised.

Keep infections away

Limit visitors in the early weeks.

Everyone should wash hands before holding the baby.

Keep anyone unwell away, and do not let people kiss the baby.

Clean the nappy area front to back at every change.

Trust yourself

You will learn your baby's cues quickly. Rest when the baby rests, and ask for help, you are not meant to do this alone. If anything ever worries you, see the companion guide on newborn danger signs.

How should I hold and support my newborn baby?
Always support the baby's head and neck with your hand or arm whenever lifting, holding, or carrying. Newborn neck muscles are weak and cannot support the heavy head on their own for several months.

Always lay your baby flat on their back on a firm mattress in a separate crib or bassinet in your room. Avoid pillows, quilts, soft toys, loose blankets, and sleeping together on a couch or armchair to prevent suffocation and SIDS.

Keep the stump clean and dry at all times. Fold the top of the diaper down below the cord to expose it to air. Do not apply oil, turmeric, powders, or antiseptics unless specifically instructed by your paediatrician.

Dress your baby in one more layer of clothing than you are comfortably wearing for the room temperature. Feel their chest or upper back to gauge warmth; hands and feet naturally feel cooler due to developing circulation.

Give gentle sponge baths until the umbilical cord stump has naturally fallen off and healed. Thereafter, a gentle warm water bath 2 to 3 times a week is sufficient, as daily soaping can dry out sensitive newborn skin.

faqs.question: What is the fertile window and how is it calculated?
faqs.answer: The fertile window comprises the 5 days leading up to ovulation plus ovulation day itself. Sperm can survive inside the female reproductive tract for up to 5 days, whereas the released egg survives for 12–24 hours.

faqs.question: When is the best time to have intercourse to get pregnant?
faqs.answer: Having intercourse every 2 to 3 days throughout the month ensures continuous sperm viability, while having sex on the day of ovulation and the 2 days prior offers the highest mathematical probability of conception.

faqs.question: Why should women take folic acid before getting pregnant?
faqs.answer: Taking 400 mcg of folic acid daily starting at least 1 month before conception prevents major neural tube birth defects of the baby's brain and spine (like spina bifida and anencephaly) by up to 70%.

faqs.question: How long does it typically take a healthy couple to conceive?
faqs.answer: About 80% to 85% of healthy couples conceive within 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse, and about 90% within 2 years. Taking several months is completely standard.

faqs.question: What are the essential nutrients for an Indian postpartum diet?
faqs.answer: High-quality protein (dal, paneer, eggs, sprouts, fish) for tissue repair; iron (green vegetables, dates, jaggery) to replenish blood loss; calcium (milk, curd, ragi) for bone density and milk production; and warm fluids for hydration.

faqs.question: Are traditional foods like panjiri and gond laddoos safe after delivery?
faqs.answer: Yes, in moderation. These traditional preparations provide concentrated calories, healthy fats, and galactagogues beneficial for nursing mothers. Avoid excessive ghee and sugar which can trigger digestive sluggishness or rapid weight gain.

faqs.question: How many extra calories does a nursing mother need?
faqs.answer: Breastfeeding burns significant energy, requiring an additional 450 to 500 nutrient-rich calories per day compared to pre-pregnancy needs, along with at least 2.5 to 3 liters of water daily.

faqs.question: What foods should be avoided or limited after delivery?
faqs.answer: Avoid crash dieting, deep-fried or ultra-processed snacks, excessive caffeine (tea/coffee), and gas-producing raw foods if they cause digestive distress or infant colic.

faqs.question: How soon after delivery can I safely start exercising to lose weight?
faqs.answer: Gentle walking and pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises can begin as soon as comfortable. Formal abdominal or aerobic workouts should wait until your 6-week postpartum checkup and clearance from your gynaecologist.

Recover stronger with the right food - MiGynae App

Recovery diet, breastfeeding help and doctor-backed guidance in one place.

What you eat after delivery helps you heal, feel stronger, and feed your baby well. Here is a simple, Indian-friendly guide to eating for recovery.

After delivery your body is healing, making milk, and running low on sleep. The right food gives you energy, speeds recovery, and supports breastfeeding. This is not the time to diet - it is the time to nourish.

Build these into every day

Protein - dal, paneer, eggs, sprouts, chicken or fish. It repairs your body and builds stamina.

Iron - green leafy veg, dates, jaggery. It rebuilds the blood lost at delivery.

Calcium - milk, curd, ragi, til. Important while breastfeeding.

Fibre - vegetables, fruit, whole grains. Keeps digestion easy and prevents constipation.

Warm fluids - water, soups, milk. They support recovery and milk supply.

Indian staples that help

Panjiri / gond laddoo - traditional energy foods, in moderation

Ajwain water and jeera water - may ease digestion and gas

Dahi, dalia, khichdi - light, warm and easy to digest

Enjoy ghee and rich foods in small amounts - your body needs nourishment, not heaviness.

Limit or avoid

Go easy on:

  • Too much ghee or oil
  • Junk food and excess sweets
  • Foods that trigger acidity or gas for you
  • Too much tea, coffee or caffeine
  • Crash diets to lose weight quickly

Eating for your milk supply

If you are breastfeeding, what you eat and drink matters even more. The MiGynae App has breastfeeding tips and foods that support your milk supply - read them alongside this diet.

A few simple tips

Eat small meals often rather than three heavy ones.

Keep water beside you, and sip every time you feed the baby.

Keep healthy snacks within reach for hungry feeding hours.

Weight comes off slowly and naturally - be patient with your body.

Be kind to yourself

Some days you will eat well, some days you will just manage. That is okay. Let family help with cooking so you can rest and feed. A well-fed mother recovers faster.

Healing, not just eating

Good food is one part of recovery. Also read the post-delivery recovery guide in the MiGynae App - it covers healing after both a normal delivery and a caesarean, step by step.

title: Low-Lying Placenta: What It Means and What to Do

excerpt: Told your placenta is low-lying? Learn what it means, why it usually moves up, precautions to take, bleeding warning signs, and what it means for delivery.
imageAlt: Pregnant woman talking with her doctor about a low-lying placenta, with a diagram of the baby and placenta in the uterus

faqs.question: What is a low-lying placenta (placenta previa)?
faqs.answer: A low-lying placenta occurs when the placenta attaches in the lower portion of the uterus, lying within 2 centimeters of the internal cervical os (opening) or partially/completely covering it.

faqs.question: Will a low-lying placenta move up as pregnancy progresses?
faqs.answer: Yes, in more than 90% of cases diagnosed at the 18–20 week anomaly scan, the placenta migrates upward and away from the cervix as the upper uterine muscular wall expands into the third trimester.

faqs.question: What precautions must I take if diagnosed with a low-lying placenta?
faqs.answer: Avoid heavy lifting, strenuous physical workouts, vaginal intercourse (pelvic rest), and prolonged bumpy journeys. Ensure you rest adequately and keep your doctor's emergency contact accessible.

faqs.question: What is the primary danger sign of placenta previa?
faqs.answer: Sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester. Even a slight streak of red blood or spotting requires immediate emergency hospital assessment.

faqs.question: Can I have a normal delivery if my placenta remains low-lying?
faqs.answer: If the placenta remains within 2 centimeters of the cervix or covers the internal opening at term (36–37 weeks), a planned caesarean section is required for maternal and fetal safety to prevent severe intrapartum hemorrhage.

content:
Understand your reports, without the worry - MiGynae App

Scan explainers, week-by-week tracking and doctor-backed guidance in one place.

A low-lying placenta sounds scary, but it is common and usually settles on its own. Here is what it means, what to watch for, and when to get help.

What it means

The placenta is your baby's lifeline. Low-lying means it has settled in the lower part of the uterus, near or over the cervix (the opening). It is usually found on a routine scan - not because anything is wrong.

The good news first

A low placenta at the 18-22 week scan is very common. As the uterus grows, it usually moves up and away on its own by the third trimester. Only a small number stay low - so a low report early on is rarely a reason to worry.

What to do - and avoid

Do:

  • Go for your repeat scan (usually around 32 weeks) to recheck the position.

Rest more, and keep your doctor's number handy.

Keep all your scan reports together.

Avoid (if your doctor advises):

  • Heavy lifting and hard exercise
  • Intercourse
  • Long travel, especially later in pregnancy
  • Ignoring even a small amount of bleeding

Your doctor will tell you how careful to be, based on how low it is.

Track your baby, and your body

Two free tools in the MiGynae App help you here. Use the kick tracker to keep an eye on your baby's movements. And use the contraction tracker - with a low placenta, tightenings or contractions can set off bleeding, so if you feel any, time them and head in. Keep both handy.

Go to the hospital at once if you have

The main warning sign is bleeding - do not wait:

  • Any vaginal bleeding, even painless or light
  • Bright red bleeding, with or without clots
  • Tightening, cramps or belly pain
  • Reduced baby movements
  • Feeling very dizzy or faint

About your delivery

If the placenta moves up in time, a normal delivery is usually possible. If it stays low and covers the opening near your due date, your doctor will plan a caesarean for safety. This is a planned, protective choice - not a failure.

Questions to ask your doctor

So you feel clear and calm:

  • How low is my placenta, and is it covering the opening?
  • What activities should I avoid right now?
  • When is my repeat scan?
  • What should I do if I notice any bleeding?

faqs.question: मासिक चक्र (पीरियड) सामान्य तौर पर कितने दिन का होता है?
faqs.answer: सामान्य मासिक चक्र आमतौर पर 21 से 35 दिनों का होता है, और रक्तस्राव 2 से 7 दिनों तक रहता है। जीवनशैली या तनाव की वजह से 2-3 दिन का अंतर सामान्य माना जाता है।

faqs.question: पीरियड में बहुत ज़्यादा ब्लीडिंग कब मानी जाती है?
faqs.answer: अगर आपको हर 1 से 2 घंटे में पैड बदलना पड़े, बड़े खून के थक्के (clots) निकलें, या अत्यधिक कमज़ोरी और चक्कर महसूस हों, तो यह असामान्य भारी रक्तस्राव (Menorrhagia) है और डॉक्टर की सलाह ज़रूरी है।

faqs.question: क्या तनाव के कारण पीरियड देर से आ सकते हैं?
faqs.answer: हाँ। अत्यधिक मानसिक या शारीरिक तनाव से कॉर्टिसोल हार्मोन बढ़ता है, जो ओव्यूलेशन (अंडे के बनने) को रोक या टाल सकता है, जिससे पीरियड देर से आते हैं या रुक जाते हैं।

faqs.question: अनियमित पीरियड के लिए डॉक्टर को कब दिखाना चाहिए?
faqs.answer: अगर चक्र लगातार 21 दिन से कम या 35 दिन से ज़्यादा हो, लगातार 3 महीने पीरियड न आए, असहनीय दर्द हो, या दो पीरियड के बीच ब्लीडिंग हो, तो तुरंत गाइनोकोलॉजिस्ट को दिखाएँ।

content:
अपने चक्र को स्मार्ट तरीके से ट्रैक करें - MiGynae App

जानें कि आपके लिए क्या सामान्य है, और डॉक्टर-भरोसेमंद जवाब पाएँ।

आपका पीरियड एक मासिक स्वास्थ्य जाँच है। यहाँ है कि क्या सामान्य है, क्या नहीं, और डॉक्टर को कब दिखाना है।

पहले, क्या सामान्य है

चक्र आमतौर पर हर 21 से 35 दिन में आता है, और रक्तस्राव लगभग 2 से 7 दिन रहता है। पीरियड शुरू होने के पहले एक-दो साल में थोड़ी अनियमितता बिल्कुल सामान्य है।

डॉक्टर को कब दिखाएँ

अगर आपको यह हो तो पीरियड की जाँच ज़रूरी है:

  • बहुत तेज़ रक्तस्राव हर 1 से 2 घंटे में पैड भीगना, या बड़े थक्के
  • पीरियड 7 दिन से ज़्यादा चलना
  • चक्र बार-बार 21 दिन से कम या 35 दिन से ज़्यादा
  • 3 महीने या उससे ज़्यादा पीरियड न आना (और आप गर्भवती न हों)
  • पीरियड के बीच या संबंध के बाद रक्तस्राव
  • इतना दर्द कि रोज़ का काम रुक जाए
  • 15 साल की उम्र तक पीरियड बिल्कुल न आना

घरेलू उपाय जो मदद करते हैं

ऐंठन के लिए पेट के निचले हिस्से पर गर्म सिकाई रखें

पानी पीती रहें, और गर्म अदरक या अजवाइन का पानी पिएँ

मासिक चक्र (पीरियड) सामान्य तौर पर कितने दिन का होता है?
सामान्य मासिक चक्र आमतौर पर 21 से 35 दिनों का होता है, और रक्तस्राव 2 से 7 दिनों तक रहता है। जीवनशैली या तनाव की वजह से 2-3 दिन का अंतर सामान्य माना जाता है।
पीरियड में बहुत ज़्यादा ब्लीडिंग कब मानी जाती है?
अगर आपको हर 1 से 2 घंटे में पैड बदलना पड़े, बड़े खून के थक्के (clots) निकलें, या अत्यधिक कमज़ोरी और चक्कर महसूस हों, तो यह असामान्य भारी रक्तस्राव (Menorrhagia) है और डॉक्टर की सलाह ज़रूरी है।
क्या तनाव के कारण पीरियड देर से आ सकते हैं?
हाँ। अत्यधिक मानसिक या शारीरिक तनाव से कॉर्टिसोल हार्मोन बढ़ता है, जो ओव्यूलेशन (अंडे के बनने) को रोक या टाल सकता है, जिससे पीरियड देर से आते हैं या रुक जाते हैं।
अनियमित पीरियड के लिए डॉक्टर को कब दिखाना चाहिए?
अगर चक्र लगातार 21 दिन से कम या 35 दिन से ज़्यादा हो, लगातार 3 महीने पीरियड न आए, असहनीय दर्द हो, या दो पीरियड के बीच ब्लीडिंग हो, तो तुरंत गाइनोकोलॉजिस्ट को दिखाएँ।

faqs.question: PCOD और PCOS में मुख्य अंतर क्या है?
faqs.answer: PCOD एक आम स्थिति है जिसमें अंडाशय में अपरिपक्व अंडे सिस्ट का रूप ले लेते हैं, जिसे सही डाइट से सुधारा जा सकता है। PCOS एक गंभीर एंडोक्राइन और मेटाबॉलिक सिंड्रोम है जिसमें हार्मोन का भारी असंतुलन, इंसुलिन रेजिस्टेंस और मुँहासे/बालों की समस्या होती है।

faqs.question: क्या PCOS में प्रेग्नेंट होना संभव है?
faqs.answer: हाँ। सही खानपान, वज़न नियंत्रण, नियमित व्यायाम और डॉक्टर की देखरेख में ओव्यूलेशन ट्रैकिंग से PCOS और PCOD से जूझ रही महिलाएँ भी आसानी से स्वस्थ गर्भधारण कर सकती हैं।

faqs.question: PCOS के प्रमुख लक्षण क्या हैं?
faqs.answer: अनियमित या बंद पीरियड, चेहरे और ठोड़ी पर अनचाहे बाल (Hirsutism), जिद्दी मुँहासे, सिर के बालों का झड़ना, और पेट के आसपास तेजी से वज़न बढ़ना इसके मुख्य लक्षण हैं।

faqs.question: PCOS की जाँच के लिए कौन से टेस्ट किए जाते हैं?
faqs.answer: पेल्विक अल्ट्रासाउंड (अंडाशय की जाँच के लिए) और ब्लड टेस्ट (फास्टिंग इंसुलिन, टेस्टोस्टेरोन, LH, FSH, थायरॉइड और प्रोलैक्टिन) से PCOS का सटीक निदान होता है।

PCOS महिलाओं की सबसे आम हार्मोन स्थितियों में से एक है, और अक्सर नज़रअंदाज़ हो जाती है। यहाँ है कि खुद की जाँच कब कराएँ।

PCOD और PCOS एक जैसे नहीं हैं

PCOD: अंडाशय (ovaries) में कई छोटे, अधूरे follicles होते हैं और पीरियड अनियमित हो सकते हैं। यह आम है और अक्सर हल्का होता है।

PCOS: PCOD के साथ-साथ हार्मोन के कई लक्षण - जैसे मुँहासे, अनचाहे बाल, वज़न बढ़ना और अनियमित चक्र। यह एक बड़ी स्थिति है जिसकी करीबी देखभाल चाहिए।

छोटे में: PCOS यानी PCOD साथ में लक्षण। दोनों आम हैं, और दोनों संभाले जा सकते हैं।

किन संकेतों पर ध्यान दें

अनियमित, देर से या गायब पीरियड

मुँहासे, या तैलीय त्वचा जो ठीक न हो

चेहरे, ठोड़ी या शरीर पर अनचाहे बाल

सिर के बालों का पतला होना

वज़न बढ़ना, या पेट के आसपास वज़न घटाने में कठिनाई

गर्दन या बगल में गहरे, मखमली धब्बे

जाँच कब कराएँ

अगर इनमें से कुछ संकेत एक साथ दिखें, या आपके पीरियड पहले एक-दो साल के बाद भी अनियमित रहें, तो स्त्री रोग विशेषज्ञ को दिखाएँ। एक साधारण जाँच - आपका इतिहास, एक स्कैन और कुछ ब्लड टेस्ट - से पता चल जाता है। जितनी जल्दी पता चले, संभालना उतना आसान।

faqs.answer: फाइबर और प्रोटीन से भरपूर खाना: मिलेट (बाजरा, ज्वार, रागी), हरी सब्जियाँ, मूंग दाल, स्प्राउट्स, पनीर और अंडे खाएँ। मैदा, सफेद चीनी, पैकेटबंद नमकीन और तली चीज़ों से पूरी तरह परहेज करें।

faqs.answer: हफ्ते में 5 दिन कम से कम 30 मिनट मध्यम गति से चलें (Brisk walk), साइकिल चलाएँ या डांस करें, साथ ही हफ्ते में 2 दिन हल्का स्ट्रेंथ वर्कआउट या योग ज़रूर करें।

faqs.answer: हाँ। मेडिकल रिसर्च के अनुसार सिर्फ 5% से 10% अतिरिक्त वज़न घटाने से ही इंसुलिन रेजिस्टेंस कम होता है और ओव्यूलेशन प्राकृतिक रूप से दोबारा शुरू हो जाता है।

फाइबर और प्रोटीन से भरपूर खाना: मिलेट (बाजरा, ज्वार, रागी), हरी सब्जियाँ, मूंग दाल, स्प्राउट्स, पनीर और अंडे खाएँ। मैदा, सफेद चीनी, पैकेटबंद नमकीन और तली चीज़ों से पूरी तरह परहेज करें।
PCOS के लिए रोज़ कितनी एक्सरसाइज़ करनी चाहिए?
हफ्ते में 5 दिन कम से कम 30 मिनट मध्यम गति से चलें (Brisk walk), साइकिल चलाएँ या डांस करें, साथ ही हफ्ते में 2 दिन हल्का स्ट्रेंथ वर्कआउट या योग ज़रूर करें।
क्या वज़न घटाने से पीरियड नियमित हो सकते हैं?
हाँ। मेडिकल रिसर्च के अनुसार सिर्फ 5% से 10% अतिरिक्त वज़न घटाने से ही इंसुलिन रेजिस्टेंस कम होता है और ओव्यूलेशन प्राकृतिक रूप से दोबारा शुरू हो जाता है।

अपने उपजाऊ दिन जानें - MiGynae App

मुफ्त पीरियड और ओव्यूलेशन ट्रैकर, और गर्भधारण की कोशिश के लिए डॉक्टर-भरोसेमंद मार्गदर्शन।

जब आप बच्चे की कोशिश कर रही हों, तो कुछ आसान और प्रमाणित कदम सच में फर्क डालते हैं। यहाँ से शुरू करें - और जानें कि ऐप हर चक्र में कैसे मदद करता है।

ज़्यादातर स्वस्थ दंपतियों को गर्भधारण में समय लगता है - अक्सर कई महीने - और यह सामान्य है। कुछ आसान बातें आपकी संभावना सच में बढ़ा सकती हैं। यहाँ से शुरू करें।

अपना उपजाऊ समय (fertile window) जानें

यह सबसे बड़ी बात है। आप ओव्यूलेशन के आसपास के कुछ दिनों में सबसे ज़्यादा उपजाऊ होती हैं - आमतौर पर चक्र के बीच में। इन दिनों में संबंध का समय बाकी किसी भी चीज़ से ज़्यादा मायने रखता है।

अपने उपजाऊ दिन जानें - ट्रैक करें

MiGynae App में पीरियड और ओव्यूलेशन ट्रैकर है। अपना चक्र लॉग करें और यह आपके लिए उपजाऊ समय और ओव्यूलेशन का दिन बता देता है - ताकि आपको पता हो कि कब कोशिश करनी है। इसी चक्र से इसका उपयोग शुरू करें।

समय सही रखें

पूरे महीने हर 2 से 3 दिन में संबंध बनाएँ - इससे आपका उपजाऊ समय अपने-आप कवर हो जाता है।

ओव्यूलेशन के आसपास, उस दिन और उससे 1 से 2 दिन पहले कोशिश करें।

"एकदम सही" समय को लेकर तनाव न लें - नियमित, शांत मन से कोशिश सबसे अच्छी रहती है।

अपने शरीर को तैयार करें

गर्भधारण से पहले फोलिक एसिड शुरू करें (डॉक्टर की सलाह अनुसार) - यह शुरुआती दिनों से बच्चे की रीढ़ की रक्षा करता है।

स्वस्थ वज़न रखें - बहुत ज़्यादा और बहुत कम, दोनों प्रजनन क्षमता पर असर डालते हैं।

प्रोटीन, आयरन और फल के साथ संतुलित, घर का खाना खाएँ।

अच्छी नींद लें, रोज़ चलें-फिरें, और तनाव कम करें।

धूम्रपान और शराब छोड़ें, और कैफीन सीमित करें।

ऐप में और जानें

प्री-कंसेप्शन एक्सरसाइज़ - शरीर को तैयार करने के लिए हल्की दिनचर्या

सीड साइक्लिंग (Seed cycling) - कोशिश के दौरान कई महिलाएँ अपनाती हैं, एक पोषण दिनचर्या

गर्भधारण से पहले की जाँचें - ब्लड टेस्ट और जाँचों की सूची जो डॉक्टर सुझा सकते हैं

डॉक्टर को कब दिखाएँ

सिर्फ इंतज़ार न करें, जल्दी जाँच कराएँ अगर:

  • आपकी उम्र 35 से कम है और 12 महीने से कोशिश कर रही हैं
  • आपकी उम्र 35 या उससे ज़्यादा है और 6 महीने से कोशिश कर रही हैं
  • आपके पीरियड अनियमित या बंद हैं, या आपको PCOS, थायरॉइड या कोई और स्थिति है
  • आपके गर्भपात हुए हों, या कोई पेल्विक सर्जरी या संक्रमण हुआ हो

कोशिश से लेकर गर्भावस्था तक: • उपजाऊ समय बताने वाला पीरियड और ओव्यूलेशन ट्रैकर • प्री-कंसेप्शन एक्सरसाइज़ और सीड साइक्लिंग • गर्भधारण से पहले की जाँचों की सूची • पॉज़िटिव आने पर शुरुआती गर्भावस्था का मार्गदर्शन

content:
नवजात के खतरे के संकेत हमेशा साथ रखें - MiGynae App

खतरे के संकेत, दूध पिलाने में मदद और डॉक्टर-भरोसेमंद नवजात मार्गदर्शन, हमेशा साथ।

नवजात जल्दी बीमार हो सकते हैं। इन संकेतों को जानना और तुरंत कदम उठाना आपके बच्चे की जान बचा सकता है। अपनी समझ पर भरोसा करें।

बच्चे में यह हो तो तुरंत डॉक्टर के पास जाएँ

इनमें से किसी एक के लिए भी तुरंत मेडिकल देखभाल ज़रूरी है:

  • साँस में तकलीफ तेज़ या आवाज़ वाली साँस, पसलियाँ अंदर धँसना, घुरघुराहट, या होंठ/जीभ नीले
  • दूध न पीना, या बहुत कम पीना
  • बहुत सुस्त, ढीला, या मुश्किल से जागना
  • झटके या ऐंठन (fits)
  • बुखार, या शरीर छूने में ठंडा
  • गहरा पीलापन, या हथेली और तलवों का पीला होना
  • नाभि का लाल, सूजा, बदबूदार या पस निकलता होना
  • लगातार उल्टी, पेट का फूला-कठोर होना, या पेशाब/मल न आना
  • कमज़ोर, तेज़ (चीख जैसी), या लगातार रोना

तुरंत क्या करें

इंतज़ार न करें। बच्चे को तुरंत अपने डॉक्टर या नज़दीकी अस्पताल ले जाएँ।

रास्ते में बच्चे को गर्म रखें, अपनी छाती से skin-to-skin।

अस्पताल के कागज़ साथ रखें, और हो सके तो पहले फोन कर दें।

डॉक्टर की सलाह के बिना कोई घरेलू नुस्खा या दवा न दें।

जब तक डॉक्टर तक पहुँचें

  • साँस मुश्किल या होंठ नीले: बच्चे को सीधा अपनी छाती से लगाएँ, नाक धीरे से साफ़ करें, और जल्दी निकलें।
  • झटके/ऐंठन: बच्चे को करवट लिटाएँ, मुँह में कुछ न डालें, और ध्यान दें कि यह कितनी देर रहा।
  • छूने में ठंडा: skin-to-skin और टोपी से धीरे-धीरे गर्म करें, और दोनों को ढकें।
  • बुखार: कसकर न लपेटें, बच्चे को ठंडा और आरामदेह रखें।
  • जाग रहा और पी सकता है: स्तनपान कराती रहें। झटके आ रहे हों या बहुत सुस्त हो तो कभी ज़बरदस्ती न पिलाएँ।

शक हो तो जाँच कराएँ

आप अपने बच्चे को सबसे अच्छा जानती हैं। डॉक्टर को दिखाकर आश्वस्त होना, इंतज़ार करने से हमेशा बेहतर है। नवजात के मामले में मदद माँगने में कभी झिझक न करें।
